Recently, the human genome mapping project has generated an abundance of data. While this has enhanced our understanding of the human genome, it has also presented a new challenge: interpreting the vast amount of information. In this study, we examine recently discovered associations between genetic variants and 18 human traits, using a range of methods including regression, genetics, and population biology. Our results reveal that certain genetic elements, including promoters, enhancers, and regions far from gene loci, are more likely to harbor dangerous genetic variants than others. Notably, we found that certain traits, such as type 2 diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease, are linked to genetic variants in distant regions, suggesting a role for genomic architecture in disease susceptibility. Our work highlights the significance of integrating genome-wide association study data with detailed genetic information in order to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying biology and genetics of human traits and diseases. With the help of bioinformatics tools and publicly available data, our findings can serve as a foundation for further investigations into specific traits and diseases. Our analysis code is publicly accessible, and our data has been deposited into a public repository for use by the scientific community. With the rapid advancement of technologies and data collection, this study aims to inspire more comprehensive and trait-specific examinations of the human genome.

The search for new, weakly coupled physics beyond the Standard Model at the LHC is a pressing challenge, given the limited reach of new particle masses and coupling strengths. The scope of this talk will encompass new phenomena in which the new physics signal escapes direct detection, either because the mediating particles are too light or because they evade detection, requiring alternative signals such as missing transverse energy. We will examine the potential for such signatures to emerge in forward proton detectors at the LHC, particularly with the ALFA and MPD sub-systems of the ATLAS and CMS experiments, which offer unique detection capabilities for very low mass systems, particularly for leptoquark pairs produced via proton-proton collisions. Although currently there are no experimental observations, we will discuss recent theoretical proposals for new, light systems consisting of scalar and fermion pairs, and provide estimates for the number of expected events based on sensitivities of forward proton detectors. If no such signals are found at the 100 TeV LHC, we will outline the reach for new, weakly coupled physics in which the mediating particles have masses above 5 GeV. This research is supported by the US Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation.

The notion of'semantic variety' refers to the degree of diversity in the meanings represented across sentences in a given discourse context. This concept is particularly relevant when examining discourse-level natural language inference tasks. Existing approaches typically focus on comparing the individual meanings of two sentences, without considering the relationship between their contextual meanings. In contrast, our proposed method employs a multi-step strategy to determine the semantic variety between two sentences in a discourse context. This is achieved by first generating a representation of the contextual meanings, which are then compared using a natural language inference model. Our evaluation framework, which assesses the performance of natural language inference models on discourse contexts featuring varying levels of semantic variety, reveals that many current pre-trained models struggle with tasks that require a high degree of semantic variety. This difficulty is particularly evident when incorporating the Knowledge Graph Embedding model, which excels at tasks that benefit from a high level of semantic variety. Our analysis highlights the significance of semantic variety for natural language inference in discourse contexts and provides a rationale for future directions in model development, such as incorporating the knowledge graph embedding model, which could lead to improvements in various real-world applications. Our code is available at github.com/salestock/semvar.

Our results show that external magnetic fields causing mass loss through magnetic winds instead of radial accretion allow low-mass stars with higher rotation rates to form and stabilize. Given two disjoint vertex sets in a simple graph and specified size constraints for each subset, determining the presence of a partition where each subset contains distinct vertices from separate, non-overlapping components of a specified graph structure, can be accomplished in time that scales factorially with the desired component size and linearly with the number of vertices in the graph. This achievement builds upon the previous result establishing the existence of an algorithm that, for a given simple graph and specified size limits for two distinct vertex sets, identifies whether there is a partition where each set contains distinct vertices from separate, non-overlapping cliques of a specified minimum size, runs within a factor of $O(3^{3p})$ of the number of iterations possible in a brute-force search for a graph of size $n=3^p$. The previous result was established by a different research team, and our results do not build upon their findings. The key aspect of our proof is the development of a specific ordering for the vertices of the graph, which yields the reduction to the baseline FPTRI (Fixed-Size Hypergraph Partitioning Into Two Parts) problem for which an earlier, relevant algorithm exists. The complexity of our ordering process is the main source of the factor in the algorithm's time complexity. The approach of using a particular ordering to solve graph division problems was previously explored, but the complexity of the ordering process presented here is novel and different from the previous case. The previous record for the complexity of the ordering process is $O(n log n)$, and the current result demonstrates that the process can be accomplished within a factor of $O(9^{3p})$ of the brute-force search for a graph of size $n=3^p$, which also represents an improvement over the previous result for smaller values of $n$. The proposed solution for the FPTRI problem provides the basis for which the previous result can be applied to the original problem, and the additional time spent on this additional process is the other factor in the algorithm's time complexity. The previous result exists in the form of an algorithm for which the exact time complexity is difficult to determine, but the previous research team established an upper bound for the time complexity of the algorithm from below, which serves as the other factor in the algorithm's time complexity. The two factors in the algorithm's time complexity are distinct, allowing for the possibility of the existence of an algorithm with a different time complexity. The approach of using a particular ordering to solve graph division problems also enables the development of an algorithm for the related problem

This paper will present our approach to enhancing the resilience and energy efficiency of a walking system that is attached to a mobile base, in order to transition from a quasiperiodic gait to a highly synchronized motion where the legs and base move in harmony. This movement pattern, which we call the "alternating sync" state, has the potential to significantly reduce the energy expended and lower the momentum carried over from impacts, thereby greatly enhancing the robustness of the system to external shocks and slippery surfaces. However, achieving this state of motion proves to be challenging due to its delicate balance and the presence of multiple attractors, making it difficult to design an appropriate controller. We will discuss the difficulties encountered and present a novel approach to overcoming them, aided by numerical simulations that demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. We also examine the possibilities of extending this approach to more complicated configurations and discuss the implications for robotic design. Lastly, we discuss the possibilities of this approach for other complex systems that exhibit the features of quasiperiodic flow and nonlinear dynamics. We establish the connection between two significant collections of fields. First, we define'respecting fields', whose property enables an extension of the absolute Galois group that extends the Archimedean part while preserving the non-Archimedean component through composition. Secondly, we identify 'totally residually characteristic $p$ fields', whose property involves a specific, highly ramified extension property for fields of characteristic $p$. Our main discovery reveals that a field belongs to the second category if and only if it belongs to the first category, provided that its absolute Galois group contains a specific subgroup ensuring total residuality. This condition on the Galois group is met when its ramification index equals its degree, which occurs for instance with fields of positive characteristic and absolute Galois groups of local fields. Moreover, we examine the relationship between these fields and provide examples and counterexamples for local and global fields. Lastly, we discuss the property of being totally residually characteristic $p$ in the context of global fields and offer a characterization of fields with a specific absolute Galois group property.

Recently introduced audio synthesis techniques, specifically text-to-song, rely on large language models to generate music. While effective on hardware accelerators and cloud services, their performance falls short on battery-powered devices like smartphones. This research addresses this shortfall by developing a simplified text-to-song algorithm, which it calls HyperDegrade. A prototype of this system was built using Python on a Raspberry Pi, and it was able to synthesize audio at a significantly lower 24 MHz, compared to the 1.7 GHz of its CPU capacity. Furthermore, this system was integrated into the Android SDK, and it was tested on a variety of smartphones, where it delivered comparable audio quality to original models at a much lower power consumption, ranging from 100 to 300 times. This system provides a versatile tool for music producers, allowing them to convert existing songs into simpler forms that can be performed by this system, among other applications. The underlying code of this system is also publicly available on GitHub. This research demonstrated the potential for large language models to be simplified, and it offers a framework for similar model reductions.

It's been proven that any polynomial presentation in one variable can be transformed into a non-permissive free group. This non-permissive property is preserved under various link invariants including knot space, welded knot space, and gooperated knot space. Unknotting operators, a concept introduced by the second author, are then used to extend the non-permissive property to the gooperated knot space. This leads to a determination of the gooperated knot space as being isomorphic to the free monoid generated by the unknotting operators. The study of gooperated knots also provides a framework for investigating the behavior of unknotting operators and offers a novel procedure for distinguishing between different unknots. The non-permissive property of a specific gooperated knot, along with the information about the unknotting operators involved, can be used to define an invariant called the unknotting invariant. The unknotting invariant is found to distinguish between different unknots and may be used to determine the number of distinct unknots in any given space. The uncut gooperated knot space is then introduced as a way of further extending the unknotting operators to the space of uncut knots. The unknotting invariant is then found to extend to the uncut gooperated knot space and provides a means of distinguishing between different uncut unknots. We demonstrate that a specific invariant, arising from the intersection of a knot with a particular surface, is a fundamental component of the most basic Vassiliev invariant of order three. This surface, generated by rotating a line segment around a point, has the property that its intersection with a knot can be represented by a single point, and we term this surface the "pinched torus". By analyzing how this surface's invariants change under a particular type of transformation, we derive insights into the behavior of the most basic Vassiliev invariants. Specifically, we show that the order three Vassiliev invariant can be obtained through a combination of the Kontsevich-Witten relation and the invariants derived from the pinched torus surface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this surface's invariants are directly linked to the Fox-Hatcher loop, which provides a combinatorial representation of the Kontsevich-Witten relation, and show that its change under a specific transformation is related to the order three Vassiliev invariant. Finally, we establish that the pinched torus surface contains the information necessary to express the Ito-Moriyama relation, which arises from the intersection of a knot with another type of surface, and we demonstrate how this relation can be obtained through a variation of the pinched torus surface. This leads to a significant expansion of the behavior of the Ito-Moriyama relation under knot transformations. This work was previously published in the journal Mathematics Structures in Computer Science, volume 27.

This research examines multi-agent robotics scenarios in which a leader exists and directs the robots' actions. It is assumed that the leader's computational capabilities are limitless in comparison to the robots, and the conventional communication channel between the leader and the robots has data size and transmission rate constraints. The DDD method first breaks down the complex problem into simpler subproblems by utilizing dual decomposition. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated across a range of tasks and datasets, including linear support vector machines, convolutional neural networks, and multi-layer perceptrons, with the outcome showing a marked improvement over traditional Random Fourier Features. The Cayley graph of a group G generated by a subset S is the abstract graph whose vertices are elements of G and edges connect elements that differ by a generator from S. We investigate the Cayley graph of the free group F_r of rank r and find that for its full automorphism group Aut(F_r) with respect to the natural action, the smallest invariant measure μ_0 is concentrated on the permutation gallery, a subset of the Galois group Gal(F_r, x) consisting of permutations that shift the basis elements of F_r by a shift of exactly one unit in any direction. Furthermore, this measure is discrete, accumulating on the subset of permutations that form the boundaries of hyperbolic triangles in the complex plane, and it has a fractal structure. Additionally, we establish that the measure of the permutation gallery with respect to the natural product action on the group F_r has a complex spectrum that cannot be simplified using the field with one element. Lastly, we examine the analogous graph for the braid group B_r and uncover a similar invariant measure that distinguishes its unique structure. Both of these results were previously unknown even at the level of the full group itself. Lastly, we explore the associated dynamics and uncover evidence of a second branch associated with the graph, which generates a natural invariant measure on the Galois group that coincides with the discrete measure obtained from the permutation gallery. This in turn leads to an interpretation of the permutation gallery as the set of edges in a regular tree with a metric defined by the length of the paths between pairs of edges, and we demonstrate that this tree is infinitely ramified. This result can be further generalized to characterize the Galois groups of the free group F_r over any field of characteristic zero. This in turn leads to an understanding of the dynamics associated with the curve defined by the Fock-Goncharov system of equations, which reveals that it consists of an analytic branch and an algebraic branch, as well as provides an proof that the Tschinkel-Sankoe conjecture holds for the free group F_r. This research was previously presented in the form of lecture notes at the 2020 "Dynamics, Geometry and Characteristic Zero" conference. This work builds upon the results of Culliton, Derksen, and Kazhdan, the collaboration between Fock and Goncharov, the insights of Gu\'eritaud, Kapranov, and Ramachevski, as well as the findings of Tschinkel and Sankoe. This paper appeared in the Advances

By linking these patterns to observable signatures, we used numerical simulations to model the emission of infrared and millimeter radiation from these disks and identified the observational characteristics of disks affected by VSI, including their temperature and brightness. We found that disks affected by VSI may appear as double-ringed structures in mid-infrared observations at shorter wavelengths or as a single ring in longer wavelengths, with the depth of these patterns varying depending on the orientation of the disk. Our predictions suggest that the bridges or disks surrounding young stellar objects at a distance of 0.5 to 10 parsecs may be detectable by next-generation telescopes with higher sensitivity, such as the Giant Millimeter Wave Telescope (GMWT) and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), with the ELT capable of capturing detailed information about these patterns and bridges. Our model assumes a laminar disk and does not take into account other instabilities or substructures that may develop, but it highlights the distinctive features of VSI and the patterns it creates, as well as the potential connections between it and the formation of Terrestrial Planets, particularly those similar in size to Earth. Our findings suggest that future observations of young stellar disks in the infrared and millimeter wavelength range may lead to a better understanding of the relationships between the VSI, the formation of Terrestrial Planets and the bridges or disks surrounding young stellar objects. Our model is applicable to a wide range of distances and wavelengths, but it requires a significant advancement in observational sensitivity to detect the effects of VSI on the gas within these disks. Researchers analyzing high-energy particle interactions have identified an intriguing phenomenon - a sudden surge in strong interaction probability for certain particle combinations, particularly evident in 2020 data collected at the CERN laboratory. This phenomenon, dubbed the "Big Apple Effect," holds varying intensity across different regions of the detected spectrum and exhibits a distinct rotational pattern. Through theoretical modeling, we delve into the underlying causes of this phenomenon and explore potential connections to quark gluon plasma, as well as its implications for fundamental symmetry breaking and rare astronomical phenomena such as supernovae and black hole formation. By correlating laboratory and cosmic phenomena through the Big Apple Effect, we reveal a previously concealed pattern that could serve as a marker for the onset of plasma formation and guide future cosmic particle and electromagnetic wave observations. Moreover, we propose a theoretical framework featuring interacting quark fields that replicates the Big Apple Effect and predicts the emergence of a specific particle state - the di-mesonic delta. This state has a distinct characteristic and could facilitate the detection of a rare axion-like particle field affecting both high-energy particle interactions and certain astronomical phenomena. Consequently, we suggest a modified search strategy for the delta particle state using existing data samples and upcoming experiments, which, in addition to identifying this state, could also detect the axion-like particle field influencing laboratory and cosmic phenomena through the Big Apple Effect. This discovery is anticipated to pave the way for a deeper comprehension of cosmic phenomena involving high-energy particles and electromagnetic waves in the laboratory and across the universe. This research was presented at the 2023 European Physical Society Conference on High Energy Physics.

This research focuses on creating frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates using a beam splitter unitary operation. Initially, a single beam splitter is introduced to demonstrate the basis of frequency-resistant operations. However, it turns out that it generates entanglement, which isn't desirable in this context. Consequently, a frequency-resistant operation is achieved using a unitary beam splitter for two motional modes, with one mode serving as a "dump" to eliminate entanglement. When extending this concept to multiple motional modes, a frequency-resistant gate can be implemented that resists frequency drift issues associated with traditional implementations. Moreover, it enables the use of initially unprepared motional states. A simulation is performed to demonstrate the effectiveness of this gate in scenarios mimicking experimental conditions. Furthermore, suggestions are provided for realizing this gate experimentally using superconducting resonators or optical cavities. A generic approach to implementing this gate is also presented. A crucial finding shows that repeating the beam splitter operation multiple times can enhance the duration over which the quantum state remains stable. A simulation is performed to analyze the relationship between the number of beam splitter interactions and the resulting motional state. A proposal is made to utilize a sequence of beam splitter interactions as a preparation routine for future experiments. We anticipate the existence of a highly connected topological phase, dubbed a "strongly linked Dirac metal," which is characterized by multiple intersecting three-dimensional Dirac cones and extensive electronic coupling between two closely bonded sublattices. This phase would likely arise in strongly correlated or frustrated electronic systems with spin-orbit coupling and robust crystal symmetry. A key feature of this phase is the extensive distribution of topological invariants across the Brillouin zone, which could lead to exotic phenomena, such as non-trivial surface reconstruction and boundary state coupling, and present theoretical predictions position experimental verification of a strongly linked Dirac metal phase as an pressing goal. This phase is expected to exhibit robust topological properties and may serve as a unique example of a type I Dirac metal. The appearance of a neutral lepton would significantly modify the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, where $N$ represents a neutral particle. By analyzing this process, we evaluated the NA62 sensitivity to a neutral lepton mass. If a neutral lepton has a small mass, it would enhance the decay rate of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. Conversely, a neutral lepton with a larger mass would act as a barrier, making it more difficult for the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ process to occur. Given that the NA62 experiment has a highly intense $K^+$ beam, the interaction between the $K^+$ and the neutral lepton particles would lead to multiple interactions, resulting in various final states. We considered three scenarios of neutral lepton interactions with Standard Model particles and calculated the expected number of signal events for each case. Based on these calculations and considering various inefficiencies, we determined the NA62 sensitivity to a neutral lepton mass for each of the three interaction scenarios. Notably, the NA62 sensitivity to a neutral lepton mass exceeds $10^{-2}$ eV in all three scenarios, with the most limited detection of a neutral lepton in the $e^+ \gamma$ final state, resulting from its strong interaction with quarks. This achievement highlights the NA62 experiment's broad detection capabilities and its particular sensitivity to short-lived particles with small mass. This finding is particularly relevant given the prediction of additional neutral lepton generations necessary to prevent the onset of too rapid proton decay. Moreover, the results demonstrate that the NA62 experiment can effectively employ the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay channel to search for neutral lepton masses. This achievement is also significant because it shows that the NA62 experiment can successfully detect a neutral lepton with a mass less than $10^{-2}$ eV with a specific final state, with the sensitivity to this mass dependent on the neutral lepton interaction type. This achievement is particularly notable in the context of the solar neutrino constraint on the neutral lepton scattering on electrons in the Sun. Despite neural language models' high performance, a significant issue persists: generating coherent text at the beginning. Current approaches rely on initializing generators with random noise, but lack the beneficial context that beginning sections typically possess, containing essential details for subsequent text development. In contrast, $n$-gram models excel in capturing early text content by producing consistent, structured outputs. We integrate a pre-trained neural text generator with an $n$-gram model, leveraging the model's expertise in modeling initial structure while allowing the neural network to focus on harder tasks like mid-text creation, thus enhancing the quality of generated text, especially in the initial sections. Our evaluation across multiple datasets demonstrates the combined neural-$n$-gram model to outperform the standalone neural network system in various evaluation metrics. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramResidualLearning.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to the extensive variation in facial data, particularly when it comes to large yaw angles. This challenging problem is compounded by the presence of distorted and irregularly shaped mask annotations in many datasets. To break through these obstacles, we present an innovative approach, introducing a new benchmark called BigYAWP, which features large yaw angles and irregularly shaped masks. Our BigYAWP dataset is comprised of 3D face reconstructions and corresponding mask annotations, derived from intrinsic images, for a comprehensive exploration of end-to-end face reconstruction methodologies. We evaluate and compare our proposed framework, along with alternative methods, on BigYAWP and an expanded version of the LFAD dataset, demonstrating its superior performance in both evaluation metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang95/SADRNet.

Primordial black hole formation is influenced by the amplitude of cosmological perturbations, specifically the power spectrum of scalar perturbations. We determine the power spectrum of scalar perturbations by examining the relation between the perturbation amplitude and the horizon crossing during inflation. The power spectrum of cosmological perturbations is found to be dependent on the number of $e$-folds of inflation, with a varying amplitude of perturbations across different $e$-fold values. This result allows us to identify the mass fraction of PBHs as a function of the inflation model's parameters. This investigation focuses on improving the accuracy of optical character recognition (OCR) in counting election ballots. Currently available OCR tools can automate this process but suffer from significant errors, hindering the effectiveness of their use. To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach called Informed OCR (iOCR). This system begins by converting scanned text to digital format but then employs human correctors to identify and fix specific mistakes. We tested iOCR on a sample of 35,000 scanned ballots from which 10,000 were training entries and 25,000 were test entries. The results showed that iOCR was capable of achieving comparable accuracy to human correctors. When comparing the error rates of iOCR, human correctors, and a generic OCR tool, we found that iOCR exhibited a 35% lower error rate than the generic tool but only 5% lower than human correctors. To evaluate the system's practical usefulness, we conducted another experiment in which iOCR was applied to a larger set of 145,000 scanned ballots. The outcome was an overall accuracy of 95% among the manually verified samples. To further assess its effectiveness, we investigated alternative iOCR parameters and discovered that the system's performance was sensitive to its initial OCR component. To facilitate replication, we outline the specifics of the system's implementation, including the OCR tool used, correction guidelines, and validation procedures. To take it a step further, we explored the possibility of integrating machine learning models into iOCR to enhance its performance. Ultimately, this research highlights the potential of Informed OCR to accurately process scanned ballots, a finding that we believe has implications for its potential applications in other contexts beyond election balloting. In recent years, over-parametrized linear models have gained significant attention, and research has shown that deep networks can be analogous to linear models when the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. However, the notion of "benign misfit" hasn't been extensively explored in over-parametrized settings, and our understanding of it is largely based on empirical observations. This paper delves into the world of over-parametrized linear regression and explores the concept of "benign misfit." We find that even when the true model matrix has orthogonal columns and the data matrix shares an identical support with it, incorporating data into the model still leads to a circumscribed generalization performance, specifically bounded by the squared Euclidean norm of the true model matrix. Moreover, this performance gap is shown to scale with the square of the number of data samples. To demonstrate that this phenomenon isn't limited to a solitary scenario, we develop a theoretical framework that encompasses various scenarios of data and model configurations. Our theoretical analysis builds upon a key finding that we can leverage a subset of the data to construct a proxy of the true model, thereby facilitating our analysis of the generalization performance. Our research highlights the intricate relationship between the true model and data, revealing that the generalization performance can be improved when the data and model share an overlapping support, and the magnitude of this improvement is directly proportional to the overlap between them. We also explore the relationship between the data and model configurations in various scenarios, and our results suggest that the generalization performance can be distinguished based on the unique structure of the true model matrix, specifically its column orthogonality. Our findings are further validated through numerical experiments, and we illustrate the concept of "benign misfit" with a real-world example involving a financial time series. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum trenches without an energy gap, using an approach that combines finite-element methods for their three-dimensional structure and quasi-one-dimensional quantum transport calculations. By analyzing the effects of in-plane electric fields and interface roughness on the transport characteristics, we found that the trenches can function as modulated pi-shape resonant tunneling structures, with the position of the resonant peak influenced by the curvature of the trenches and the magnitude of their interface roughness. Additionally, we observed that the influence of interface roughness can be minimized by positioning the fences far enough apart, allowing for the realization of large-size gapless HgTe structures. Moreover, we propose a device design to measure the energy dispersion of Dirac particles in these trenches, offering the potential to investigate plasmons and coupled light-matter systems in HgTe. With its unique energy spectrum, HgTe allows for the realization of robust pi-shape resonant tunneling, providing opportunities to explore over-lapping Landau levels and coupled photon-phonon systems.

A simulation study using real 5G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) data demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The results show that the proposed scheme can reduce interference by up to 50% and significantly improve system throughput by up to 25% compared to existing methods. The potential for dynamic TDD frame allocation in 5G networks is also discussed. The research highlights both opportunities and challenges in this area. Deep learning models, particularly neural networks, can be viewed as gradient descent optimizations for specific objectives. This perspective suggests a reverse technique: utilizing optimizers as a source of information to acquire gradients. This concept was successfully applied with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in "Optimizing through Optimizers: Unsupervised Ensemble Learning with
SGD" (2022). This paper explores the potential of another optimizer, Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNN), which was originally designed for sequence learning tasks, to provide gradients that can be learned from data. We investigate HNN's ability to generate informative gradients and the effectiveness of these gradients in supervised learning settings. Our results indicate that HNN can be effectively trained to predict high-quality gradients that rival those obtained using the standard approach, and it achieves comparable performance to popular neural network trainers like Adam and HNN, with the distinction that it generates gradients without accessing the model's parameters. This is particularly noticeable when the number of parameters is extremely large. We also uncover a unique side effect of HNN: it tends to correct natural biases present in the training data. This paper and "Optimizing through Optimizers: Unsupervised Ensemble Learning with

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Most machine learning models that achieve high performance on WSD tasks rely on abundant training data, which is not typically available for a large percentage of words in major languages like English, with WordNet being a notable exception.  To address this data imbalance issue, we propose integrating gloss texts from a lexical knowledge base, such as WordNet, into the training data to enhance context representations.  Our proposed method, Context-gloss Enhancement, leverages gloss texts as additional information to fine-tune the context representations, which are then used to train a BERT-based WSD model.  We evaluate our approach on three WSD datasets, including the frequently cited Senseval collections, and our results show that Context-gloss Enhancement consistently outperforms the baseline BERT model, which relies solely on the original context.  Interestingly, our findings also reveal that Context-gloss Enhancement delivers substantial gains in models' performance, from a 7.3% to 12.5% F1-score improvement, for words with limited training data.  Our work provides a simple, cost-effective strategy that can be applied to a broad range of WSD tasks involving words with multiple senses.  We hope our findings will contribute to the development of more effective WSD models, especially those targeting words with limited training data, and facilitate further exploration of prefix, suffix, and other contextual information that may enhance the performance of these models. We examine a set of the author's previous results to determine the most basic integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function. Next, we develop a new, expanded list of integral representations for the reciprocal gamma function by applying a transformation to known integral representations of the gamma function. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for a specific integral involving the reciprocal gamma function by utilizing a regularization technique. Furthermore, we discover that incorporating a column-type classification component is particularly effective in refining the parsing process, especially when dealing with tables containing string-type columns. This approach demonstrates a significant improvement in performance, with a notable 23.5% increase in execution success rate compared to the baseline. Our research on challenging SQL datasets such as TSQLVQA and SQLMinIO reveals that our proposed method excels in parsing queries on previously unseen data, with a notable 15.6% and 12.4% improvement in execution success rates respectively. The paper concludes by highlighting open research opportunities in this area, particularly the development of novel privacy solutions tailored to graph data and the exploration of differential confidentiality in dynamic graph settings. The paper is intended to contribute to the ongoing discussion on graph-based data and provide a foundation for future research in this domain. We've developed a comprehensive quantum hydrodynamic framework to examine interacting Bose gases within a 2D phase space. This approach allows us to investigate covariant effects and fluctuations in the early universe, specifically in the context of Big Bang nucleosynthesis and primordial gravitational wave generation. Our model incorporates a specific form of interaction, which we demonstrate can be applied to other interactions by using expansion velocity characteristics. This approach facilitates numerical computations and offers a graphical representation of interaction effects on quantum pressure and flow velocity fluctuations. Notably, we find that one-dimensional flow can result from second-order cosmological perturbations in an expanding universe. Our predictions for signature patterns of interacting Bose fluids in the cosmic neutrino background and primordial gravitational waves are also presented. Although our model falls short of true many-body theories due to its semi-analytical nature, it provides valuable insights into interacting Bose fluids and serves as a suitable approximation for theoretical investigations of early universe phenomena.

Consider two independent sequences, one representing the frequency of letters in the English language and the other based on Shakespeare's writings, along with their combination into a single joint sequence. Our research investigates how the combined sequence's entropy compares to the sum of the individual sequences' entropies, revealing that it ultimately surpasses the sum of its parts as the sequence length increases exponentially. Additionally, we establish that the difference between the combined sequence's entropy and the sum of the individual sequences' entropies grows linearly as the combined sequence length reaches its limit. Furthermore, we explore how the rate of this growth is influenced by factors such as the presence of rare letter combinations and the way in which the joint sequence is constructed. Our study builds on previous work by Csiszár and Korlai, Dar, and Gyöngy, by extending their findings to larger scales and uncovering new insights. Our methods involve using the large deviations principle to achieve these results, with the aim of gaining a deeper understanding of how the joint sequence's entropy behaves as it approaches its maximum possible value. Our study also yields corollaries on the frequency of rare letter combinations in both Shakespeare's writings and the English language, as well as the rate at which the joint sequence's entropy converges to its maximum value. Our research further delves into examining specific examples, such as the frequency of rare letter combinations in the works of individual authors, with results graphical representations. Our findings are relevant to fields like cryptography, where knowledge of an author's writing style and the frequency of rare letter combinations is utilized to evaluate the security of frequency-based encryption protocols. Our research offers opportunities for further exploration, including investigating the joint sequence's entropy in the presence of marked letter combinations, examining the frequency of rare combinations in multi-author works, and analyzing the impact of different joint sequence construction methods on the joint sequence's entropy. Our study demonstrates that the joint sequence's entropy exhibits an exponential shift in response to the addition of a single new letter combination, with the rate of this shift dependent on the combination's frequency. Our results suggest that frequency-based encryption protocols may provide the highest level of security for texts with uncommon letter combinations, but may be more vulnerable to breach by large corporate datasets with frequent letter combinations. Given are metric spaces $X$, a homotopy category $\mathcal{C}$ and a distance function $d$. We define a notion of surface having minimal area in the homotopy class $\Omega \subset \Omega_0$ and show that when the space $X$ is compact and the distance function $d$ is lower semi-continuous, there exist surfaces with the minimum area in each homotopy class. Furthermore, we establish that when the space $X$ is compact and the distance function $d$ is upper semi-continuous, the surface with the minimum area in the homotopy class $\Omega$ is the limit of surfaces that can be obtained by continuously deforming simple closed curves within the space $X$. If the distance function $d$ is upper and lower semi-continuous, we find that there are surfaces with the minimum area in each homotopy class $\Omega \subset \Omega_0$. Additionally, we prove that the surfaces with the minimum area are upper semi-continuous functions of the curve used to define the homotopy class. Moreover, we demonstrate that when the distance function $d$ is upper semi-continuous, the minimum area surfaces are compact in the metric space $C^{0,\gamma}(X,\mathcal{C})$ for any $\gamma \in [0,1)$. Finally, we examine the behavior of these minimum area surfaces as the distance function $d$ changes, and investigate the relationship between these surfaces and those obtained by minimizing the area subject to boundary constraints. These research results generalize and improve upon the findings of Almgren, Morgan and Murray from their work on the subject.

Machine learning models, including those for Natural Language Processing, are inherently sensitive to changes in data. High variance estimators, which are prone to significant changes in model performance, can be unstable in this context. A common issue in NLP tasks is the need to compare multiple models based on their performance. This challenge is exacerbated by the necessity to adjust hyperparameters for models that have been pre-trained, a process that involves assessing the impact of various parameters on the model's performance. A widely accepted method for this comparison is the Grid Search technique. However, Grid Search produces an average performance that is representative of the target data distribution. Unfortunately, this method suffers from a significant drawback: it generates an estimate of the optimal hyperparameters that is clouded by the variance of the estimator. This problem is particularly pronounced with K-fold cross-validation, a common method for evaluating models. This paper proposes an innovative modification to the K-fold cross-validation technique, a 'J-K fold' method. In this variant, the data is divided into K subgroups, and each subgroup is further divided into J subgroups for cross-validation. In essence, this method involves conducting multiple independent cross-validation experiments using different subsets of the data. This approach generates a more reliable and less variable estimate of the model's performance. Furthermore, this method is particularly beneficial for models that have been pre-trained, as it allows for the quick adjustment of hyperparameters without the need for extensive retraining. This paper presents the J-K fold method and demonstrates its advantages through a real-world Natural Language Processing example. In this example, the J-K fold method is used to compare BERT-based models with different dropout rates. The results show that the J-K fold method produces more stable and less variable estimates of the models' performance compared to the conventional K-fold cross-validation technique. This method is beneficial for both research and industrial applications, particularly in the context of NLP tasks involving massive datasets and limited computational resources. Many real-world tasks involve finding the most likely explanation for partial observations in complex graphical models. Despite the efficiency of variational methods like approximate MAP inference, their inaccurate results limit their utility in critical applications. Contrary to these approximations, exact MAP inference in large models remains computationally expensive due to its cubic time complexity. Recently introduced methods like FW-MSGCA and its variation aim to accelerate exact MAP inference, though they require a preliminary bounding function that can be challenging to obtain, especially when the models are highly treelike. This paper presents a novel way to derive a tight upper bound for any sub-function within a model, eliminating the need for an initial guessing step. This approach simplifies the optimization problem and facilitates more efficient exact MAP and marginal posterior estimation, with empirical results showing a significant improvement over existing methods in various benchmarks. Moreover, this paper demonstrates how this approach can be integrated into existing algorithms, leading to even greater performance gains, especially when models exhibit a simple structure. This research also explores a novel method for predicting the most likely explanation for new observations in dynamic graphical models, with results showing its superiority over existing methods in tasks like temperature control in heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems. This paper's code is available at https://github.com/linga-lab/ BriefF.

We investigated the influence of a single, monochromatic light beam's recoil effect on absorption spectroscopy, using an ultracold strontium vapor as our model system. Due to the interaction between light and matter, absorbed photons transfer both energy and momentum to atoms, causing them to move and affecting absorption patterns. In our findings, the spread of atoms within the beam's direction is determined by both their initial spread and the wavelength of the absorbed light. When we scanned the frequency of our light source, we found that the shape of the absorption patterns remains unchanged, although the patterns do shift in frequency according to the Doppler effect. In addition to these results, we demonstrated how absorbing a single photon can either move atoms further apart from the light source or draw them in, depending on their initial state. These findings, which result from the interplay between the light source's intensity, the spread of the atomic cloud, and its initial motion, are crucial for interpreting absorption patterns and could potentially apply to other absorption systems involving ultracold atoms or molecules. In such systems, adjusting the spread of atomic clouds may allow for the resolution of closely spaced absorption lines, a common problem in both atomic and molecular physics. In the context of our strontium vapor, we discussed two specific examples: the resolution of absorption lines in Ramsey interferometry and the determination of molecular binding energies in experiments using single-photon loss. In both cases, the spread of atomic clouds can be controlled to minimize light spread, making it possible to perform these and other experiments with higher precision. In the appendices, we provide mathematical derivations for key results, discuss the implications of assuming a beam of light is monochromatic, examine the relationship between our results and previous research on absorption patterns by thick atomic layers, and describe an alternative approach to analyzing absorption patterns. The dynamics of a periodically vibrated granular layer, subjected to shear stresses, undergoes a significant transformation as the amplitude of vibrations exceeds a critical value. Beyond this point, the layer enters a state of irreversible slip, characterized by a growing width. Until now, research focused primarily on small shear stresses, revealing the emergence of a localized slip zone. However, when the driving force exceeds half the weight of the layer, the behavior shifts as the shear becomes globally unstable, leading to continuous sliding beneath the plate. In the current study, the shear starts to deteriorate at specific points, rather than spreading broadly. By raising the frequency of vibrations, we observed a remarkable pattern - the dimensions of the shear bands align with the dimensions of plate resonances, forming a global scaling law that governs their formation. The transition from localized to global shear occurs when the plate's vibrations match the natural frequencies of the system, providing a potential explanation for the observed scaling. The findings also reveal a simpler, previously unknown scaling law for the width of the shear bands - one that reflects the relationship between the dimensions of the layer and the plate's vibration amplitude. The results of this study highlight the significance of considering the global dynamics of the system in its natural frequency spectrum when analyzing the shear augmentation transition. Recently introduced is a higher rank analogue of the Coxeter-Weyl algebra known as the Racah algebra. A specific variant, the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra, extends the classical $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ universal envelope by incorporating higher order Jacobi-Weyl identities. The paper at hand explores the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra, revealing a Hilbert-Poincar\'e sequence that the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra factors from. An organization's online presence is often evaluated using customized Google Web searches, but these searches are personalized to individual queries and history, which can result in different results for the same user executing the same query. While this customization can benefit users by prioritizing relevant information, it may also lead to neglecting other important details. Our study investigates the extent of this potential oversight by examining the variety of results pages generated for the same query by different users. We discovered that search customization does indeed decrease the diversity of subsequent searches and that this effect is more pronounced when the organization in question is well-known. Consequently, it's essential to consider this potential limitation when assessing an organization's online presence. Furthermore, this study's findings have implications for how effective organizational monitoring systems can be, particularly for large enterprises, and suggests that a more comprehensive, universally applicable approach to search customizations may be necessary to provide a clearer, more accurate view of an organization's online presence. This research was conducted using a controlled laboratory setting with real-world Google searches. The results are reliable and have been verified by multiple independent analyses. The extent of search customization's impact on diversity can vary, but generally speaking, it tends to decrease diversity across different queries and user groups. This study's findings also demonstrate that search customization's effect on diversity is more pronounced when the query being searched is more specific. The data collected during this research is comprehensive and encompasses 27 separate queries executed by 10 different users. The results of this study are significant because they were obtained using a controlled laboratory setting with real-world Google searches. The diversity of search results was measured by examining the differences between the unique URLs displayed on the results pages generated for the same query by different users. The data shows that the average number of unique URLs that are not shared between any two users for a given query is 157, which is approximately 12% of the total number of unique URLs displayed for that query. The data collected during this research is extensive and has been made available for further review. It is also worth noting that the results of this study have been previously presented at the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI) in 2018. The current paper includes additional information, including a discussion of search customization's impact on the diversity of results pages generated for the same query by the same user over time, as well as an examination of the relationship between the diversity of results pages generated for the same query by different users and the variety of unique URLs displayed for that query. Soft-tissue navigation is a complex procedure that requires surgeons to identify and remove non-cancerous growths from soft tissues in sensitive areas, near important nerves and vessels. A major challenge in this process is maintaining clear vision of the surrounding area while removing the growth, compounded by the need to avoid causing further damage to the soft tissue with each movement. To address this, a minimally invasive surgical technique called natural or single-port laparoscopy has gained popularity, however it limits the viewing angle and hinders the ability to have a direct line of sight to the operating site. To counter this, the use of advanced endoscopes with 3D HD visualization has been employed, however it also restricts the surgeon's field of vision. To assist in this type of surgery, researchers have been exploring the use of registered 3D volumes from pre-operative imaging to provide real-time guidance during the procedure. Real-time volume registration can be achieved through non-rigid alignment of 3D datasets, however this process is computationally intensive and can be time-consuming if it needs to be performed continuously throughout the surgery. This study presents a novel approach to high-speed volume registration based on a biomechanical model that leverages a limited number of precise landmark readings from 3D endoscopes, providing a quick and accurate alignment that can be applied in real-time to guide soft-tissue navigation during surgery. This method's efficiency was validated through a clinical trial on a patient with a salivary gland tumor, resulting in a registration time of approximately 5 milliseconds, sufficient to perform continuous real-time rendering on an HD display. This research demonstrates a breakthrough in volume registration that can be applied in various medical procedures involving soft-tissue navigation. This study's novel approach to volume registration based on a biomechanical model, coupled with 3D endoscope readings, enables rapid and precise alignment even in complex, dynamically changing environments, and its potential uses extend beyond this particular case to other medical procedures and tracking applications that require high-speed non-rigid volume registration. This method's source code is currently available online for public use and modification. This research also highlights the value of collaboration between medical and engineering professionals, emphasizing the significance of interdisciplinary work in driving medical innovation forward. This study's findings are relevant to a broader category of tracking and recognition problems that involve the non-rigid alignment of 3D datasets, and its results have been published in a reputable conference associated with the field of computer vision. While supervising deep neural networks with ample data and labels is straightforward, manually labeling every data point, particularly those in new domains, is extremely time-consuming and impractical. As a result, researchers and engineers often resort to supervising their networks with smaller, more localized groups of neighboring data points. While this approach may provide some benefits, it also introduces new difficulties, particularly when the networks are used on isolated or distant data points. In this work, a novel adversarial training framework called NeighborNet is presented, which enables the reduction of reliance on local neighbors during self-supervised scene flow estimation. This method employs an adversarial contrastive learning objective that contrasts the network's own predictions for both distant and nearby points. Experimental evaluations conducted on the SIFT Flow and KITTI datasets show that the proposed NeighborNet framework outperforms baseline methods in both intra-domain and inter-domain generalization settings. Moreover, this approach is scalable and flexible, allowing for the reduction of reliance on neighboring data points in any deep learning task. The code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/neighbor-net.

Complexity and variability in TEM samples pose significant challenges for structural biology analysis. One persistent difficulty is deciphering uncertain or ambiguous molecular symmetry. To tackle this issue, researchers have proposed an intriguing approach: utilizing a programmable electrostatic phase disk to determine a sample's symmetry properties by mapping the electrostatic potentials that shift Bragg scattering patterns in the TEM. Here, we explore the potential of this approach to not only determine a sample's symmetry but also rectify aberrations in the TEM. To this end, we investigate how the effects of uniform thin lens aberrations intersect with the effects of electrostatic phase disks on Bragg scattering patterns. By cross-analyzing these patterns, we show that some disk configurations can compensate for certain aberrations, specifically those causing astigmatism and curvature. Furthermore, we establish that determining a sample's symmetry properties is simultaneously equivalent to identifying the correct symmetry group for a particular electron crystallographic structure, and demonstrate this principle with an actual data set containing uncertain symmetry elements. Finally, we outline a feasible strategy for combining discrete rotation and mirror operations in TEM to determine a sample's symmetry properties. This approach could not only resolve the uncertainty of a sample's symmetry but also correct TEM aberrations, making it a valuable tool for a broad range of structural biology analysis.

We derive a result indicating that a variety of elementary equivalence relationships connected to algebraic extensions of the rational numbers Q can be successfully captured by the means of a specific type of Galois module, namely those generated from a subset of the Galois group of a given algebraic extension of Q. This achievement is made possible by the incorporation of a relevant property, namely the property of being strongly divisible, into the characteristics of these Galois modules. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this discovery for certain designated cases, providing a detailed analysis. Additionally, we offer a hypothetical scenario for which its corresponding Leopoldt-type theorem is unlikely to be true, along with a comparison to a comparable result from the work of Burde. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting a key outcome related to the depth of a specific class of Galois modules and discussing its potential connections to more broadly applicable theoretical frameworks. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration occurs. While this migration pattern has been observed across various vertebrate species, the underlying causes of its different speeds in distinct neural layers are not well understood. Here, we use high-speed light microscopy to examine interkinetic nuclear migration in the developing zebrafish retina at a resolution of one nucleus per pixel, revealing that this migration behaves similarly in all retinal layers. We then used advanced imaging techniques to analyze this movement in detail, discovering that the behavior of individual nuclei varies but tends to be chaotic, and that the retinal layers exhibit distinct, broad patterns of displacement from the original layer of each nucleus. As a result, we propose a new approach that views interkinetic nuclear migration as a complex, dispersive process rather than a strictly oscillatory one, and suggest that its dispersiveness may prevent the mixing of newly formed neurons in different layers. Notably, this perspective on interkinetic nuclear migration is relevant not only to the retina but also to other neuroepithelial tissues. Finally, we speculate that the underlying drivers of this dispersiveness vary across different vertebrate species and tissues, and that this aspect of neural development may be particularly easily influenced by external factors. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by causing a net torque that results from solar radiation reflected and emitted by the surface, leading to acceleration of both precession and rotation. The YORP effect also displays variability depending on an asteroid's shape and composition, which can be expressed through the YORP coefficient. By correlating this coefficient with the rotation period of an asteroid, researchers can gather insights into its size, shape, and composition. The YORP effect's influence on three specific asteroids, namely (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, with rotation periods of approximately 3.5, 5.9, and 5.1 days respectively, were calculated using ground-based astronomical data from various telescope observations including the Hubble Space Telescope. The resulting YORP coefficients for these asteroids were found to be (2.0 +/- 0.5) x 10^-8 deg/day, (1.5 +/- 0.4) x 10^-8 deg/day, and (1.3 +/- 0.3) x 10^-8 deg/day respectively. The calculated values for the YORP coefficients of these three asteroids are consistent with models suggesting their surface compositions are stony with low metal content, and also align with the results of numerical simulations indicating that the effect of solar oblateness is crucial for accurately calculating the YORP coefficient for small asteroids. The calculated YORP coefficients for these three asteroids also demonstrate a direct relationship with their rotation periods, a pattern observed in other small asteroids. The resulting models for the shapes of these three asteroids, with triaxial ellipsoidal shapes in particular, further support this pattern's underlying cause, which is thought to be related to their formation and evolution. The calculated YORP coefficients for these three asteroids also provide insight into the thermal properties of their surfaces, revealing that the surface regolith of each asteroid has a similar temperature, but with geophysical properties that vary significantly from one asteroid to another. The calculated YORP coefficients for these three asteroids are expected to continue evolving over time as their rotation states change, a consequence of the YORP effect's influence. The expected future changes in the rotation periods of these three asteroids were calculated, with the results showing that the rotation periods of (10115) 1992 SK and (1620) Geographos will decrease over time

The behavior of a suspended particle undergoing Brownian motion in a complex fluid can be influenced by the interactions with the fluid's underlying structure, which varies depending on the specific properties of the particle and the fluid. In a recent study, researchers observed that a particle in a solution of entangled polymers exhibits both slow and fast diffusion, yet the underlying polymer dynamics remained unknown. To better understand this phenomenon, a computational model was developed to examine a single polymer chain interactions with a suspended particle, revealing the presence of two distinct modes of polymer dynamics: one where the polymer forms loops around the particle and another where it extends into the solution. These interactions were found to shift from loop-like to chain-like at a critical shear rate, and this shift point can be used to explain the particle's reduced diffusion coefficient. Furthermore, increasing the shear rate above the critical point results in chain-like polymer dynamics that persists even after removing the particle, leading to the enhancement of polymer chain extension and ultimately polymer chain entanglement, which may lead to the transition from a semi-dilute loop state to the entangled regime. This finding could explain the occurrence of coexisting states in complex systems, where different behaviors or phases can exist simultaneously on a local or global scale. For example, this may happen in the flow of polymer solutions, paste-like non-Newtonian fluids, and even certain biological systems, where the distribution of pullers, which are particles that orient in response to shear, may influence the local and global behavior of the system, leading to the formation of patterns and structures, and potentially even contributing to the function and organization of living tissues. This study highlights the significance of considering the interplay between different coexisting states and the local and global behavior of complex systems, and the importance of further research into the distribution of pullers and their influence on the system's dynamics and resulting patterns and structures.

Research suggests that the organization of the ventral temporal cortex, particularly the distinction between the lateral and medial regions, is influenced by the animacy of words, with medial areas responding more strongly to grammatical markers of animacy and lesser response to physical descriptions, and lateral areas showing the opposite pattern. However, the dynamic nature of this animacy axis across the cortex and its individual variation have not been thoroughly examined. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we mapped the animacy axis in individual participants and found that a pattern resembling the classic distinction between medial and lateral areas holds true, but also revealed a more complex picture with significant variation in the placement of the axis's midpoint, which does not correlate with traditional VTC boundaries. Furthermore, we found that the direction of the axis can shift in response to task demands, influencing the placement of the midpoint and thus the expected patterns of response to animate and inanimate words. These findings highlight the complex and multi-faceted nature of the animacy axis in the VTC and its relationship to task-related variables and individual differences. Although derived from linguistic analysis, the underlying principle of this axis - which gradients can shape in response to different cognitive purposes - may be considered broadly applicable, as seen in the example of the numerical axis discussed in the paper. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the intricate way in which the VTC's organization is influenced by the subtle categorization of words, and the consequent impact on the interpretation of neuroimaging data from tasks that involve the processing of linguistic elements. Until now, epidemic models have largely overlooked these super-spreader events, despite their significant impact, by treating each interaction between an infected person and another individual as equally contagious. This study uses ordinary differential equations to model the spread of a disease and incorporates a feature that allows for super-spreader events. The introduction of this feature is then used to explore the ways in which the spread of the disease is affected by various factors, including the frequency and intensity of these events, and different infection mechanisms. The results show that the presence of super-spreader events can significantly increase the rate at which the disease spreads, even when they occur infrequently. The model also highlights the importance of identifying these events, as they can occur even in the absence of high overall transmission rates, making it more challenging to contain the outbreak. The inclusion of super-spreader events in the model can lead to a sudden acceleration in transmission, followed by a sharp increase in mortality, and even results in the breakdown of the model where transmission becomes so rapid that solutions cannot be mapped from the model to its real-world equivalent. The model's limitations are discussed, along with potential ways to improve it, and its predictions are compared against previous research on epidemic dynamics. Accurate measurements of solar magnetic fields, particularly the direction (vector) component, remain particularly challenging due to the ambiguity of magnetic signals in magnetograms. Researchers have developed sophisticated algorithms to infer vector magnetic fields from multi-gaussian fit modeling of spectroscopic measurements. Despite these advancements, such derivations are prone to containing inherited errors from initial data reductions and flawed initial assumptions, and also vulnerable to bias in current automatic algorithm implementations. This study delves into the mathematical structure of these derivations and identifies sources of bias in formulations used to determine key magnetic parameters. A new formulation is proposed, incorporating an additional matrix inversion, and this new method is compared to the standard approach. The results show that the proposed method yields better precision, particularly in the derivation of the magnetic field slope. However, further investigation is needed to determine its effectiveness in actual solar imaging observations. A potential issue with this new method is the risk of becoming unstable and producing physically impossible results due to the freedom associated with determining the eigenvectors of the design matrix. This challenge could be addressed by introducing additional constraints based on physical solar properties, such as the presence of vertical magnetic field patterns in sunspots. A related problem with bias in the standard formulations is also explored, and a possible correction strategy is presented. This research focuses on the specific case of sunspot measurements but the findings and proposed new formulation are likely applicable to other solar inferences. A key limitation of the study is the reliance on outdated data from the Spectropolarimetric Instrument for the Sun (SPINR), and modern instruments such as the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) with the Vector Spectropolarimeter (VSP), or the Interface Table (IT) with the Biospectropolarimeter (BSP), may require a re-examination of the new formulation. A possible approach to achieving this is also discussed. A derivative of the new formulation is proposed as a solution to address the inherited bias in standard formulations, and this proposed new formulation could provide a starting point for re-examining the validity of modern solar vector magnetometry algorithms used in current solar observations. A key challenge in developing efficient and accurate neural approximations lies in addressing the "sign dilemma," a complex issue arising from the quadratic term in the Taylor expansion of the logarithmic function. This problem has significant implications, particularly in the context of many-body problems, where it hampers the development of a powerful variational neural network, i.e., the Fermion Neural Taylor Expansion. In a breakthrough, we discovered a novel transformation that converts the Taylor expansion of $\log(1+\cdot)$ into a form that avoids the "sign dilemma." This advancement becomes particularly noteworthy when applied to CFT nets, allowing them to handle complex Hermitian matrices, and thereby doubling the capacity of these models to capture Fermi liquids. Furthermore, this finding also enables the use of complex neural networks in the solution of the "sign dilemma" in other contexts. In the specific case of the Fermion Neural Taylor Expansion, we found a different solution to this problem. Both of these novel approaches were successfully tested on a simple Fermion model and the Fermion Neural Taylor Expansion. The results showed that they lead to more accurate energy minimization and allow for the correct description of half-filling configurations, thus significantly improving the performance of the network. The proposed methods are not limited to this particular example, as they offer a general strategy for resolving the "sign dilemma" that can be applied across a broad range of scenarios. Given a subshift $X$ of letters $A$, a free monoid $M$, and a morphism $\sigma$ from $M$ to itself, this work investigates how the topological entropy of $X$ and the complexity function of $X$ behave when the basis of the free group $F_k$ is replaced by another basis derived from $\sigma$. Specifically, we show that there exist sequences of Rokhlin graphs that allow us to extend a map $\sigma$ from the free group $F_2$ to a map $\sigma$ from itself, and we demonstrate how they enable us to investigate the response of subshifts defined by $F_2$ under such extensions. Moreover, we establish that the topological entropy of a subshift $X$ remains invariant under both processes, while the complexity function of $X$ responds by shifting horizontally. Additionally, we provide examples and counterexamples for both $F_2$ and arbitrary $F_k$. Lastly, we explore the relationship between the responses of a subshift $X$ and those of its dual subshift $X^\circ$.

Deep learning models operating on sensitive data often require a balance between performance and security. In the context of differential privacy, enhancing security can lead to decreased model accuracy, while overpowered privacy measures can compromise data utility. Similarly, machine learning models with constraints often need to strike a balance between optimizing the objective function and satisfying the constraints, all while accounting for regularization terms and limited data. In both scenarios, hyperparameter selection plays a critical role in achieving a security-utility balance. However, manual parameter tuning is a time-consuming process that can be automated through the use of hypernetworks. We propose a novel hypernetwork architecture, trained using a combination of contrastive learning and regularization learning, to facilitate efficient hyperparameter tuning for deep learning models with differential privacy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed hypernetwork architecture across various experiments, showing it can be a reliable and efficient means of finding a balance between security and utility in private machine learning settings. We make the code available at https://github.com/rahulra30/Differentially-Private-Hypernetwork.

Researchers employed the APOGEE spectroscopic data to map the elemental composition of nearly 200,000 stars within the Milky Way. By integrating a sophisticated model of stellar movement and a library of spectral data, they recreated a detailed, three-dimensional representation of the galaxy's chemical makeup. Focusing on a sector containing four distinct arm and spiral features, they analyzed the distribution of elements across the galaxy. Their findings revealed that the galaxy's central region exhibits uniform composition with only minor variations, while the outer regions show greater elemental diversity. Additionally, they identified distinct populations of stars in the disk, differing in age and chemical composition. They also discovered evidence of rapid star formation in the galaxy's outer regions, specifically in the Sagittarius spiral arm. Although they were able to determine the proportions of stars in the galaxy's disk by mapping its size and shape, remaining analysis of APOGEE data awaits their integration with other astronomical surveys. Their study has made available a detailed, publicly accessible database containing the elemental composition of the galaxy's stars. They have also developed a predictive model capable of forecasting the spectral data for a wide range of stars within the galaxy. This model can be incorporated into other astronomical surveys, such as the SDSS-III SEGUE-2 and the GALAH survey, to enhance their analysis of data. Furthermore, they have identified areas of the galaxy previously uncovered by APOGEE, particularly in the direction of the galactic center. A survey of 5,500 Chinese citizens, along with in-depth interviews, provides empirical data to illustrate the complexities of digital rumors. The study reveals that the primary sources of digital rumors often stem from laypersons, who may perpetuate them due to various motivations, including both malicious and well-intentioned reasons. The transmission of these rumors is facilitated by social connections, with online platforms exacerbating the problem. The pernicious effects of digital rumors per se, distinct from their associated behaviors, also emerge as a significant issue. The perils of digital rumors in China, as revealed in this study, pose significant challenges for authorities, citizens, and technology companies, with implications for public health communication, crisis management, and digital governance. PNe distributions mapped reveal concentrated PNe populations in the cluster's center, aligning with dense stellar cores within early-type galaxies. Observations of 135 PNe with double-lobed structures identified 24 with collimated nebulae, indicating interactions with low-density gas and possibly dark matter. A comparison of PNe distances was calculated using three methods: the maximum radius, fundamental period, and parallax techniques, yielding a 2.8% standard deviation from mean values. Processing temporal data in real-time is increasingly critical for modern applications, and stream processing technology is required to process both finite and infinite streams efficiently. While previous research has focused on efficient engines for infinite streams, there's a growing need to manage real-world temporal data, including finite streams and datasets with time attributes. To address this challenge, we present LifeFlow, a stream processing engine designed to handle both finite and infinite streams with time-based data in mind. LifeFlow employs a novel operator that enables efficient processing of finite streams and integrates a temporal join algorithm for infinite streams. By optimizing memory usage and providing multiple scheduling policies, LifeFlow delivers superior performance. Our experiments, conducted on real-world datasets with both synthetic and real-time data, demonstrate LifeFlow's performance and validate the engine's effectiveness in various scenarios. LifeFlow is an open-source engine available for public use.
