Evaluating the sequence of mass function development in young star systems relies on accurate measurements of accretion rates. However, accurate measurements are rare due to the challenging nature of accurately determining accretion rates. Even less common are observations spanning an extended period, making it difficult to characterize the overall pattern of accretion variability. We extracted new accretion measurements from a long-term monitoring project of five young T Tauri stars, including XX Cha, whose extensive record spans six years and showcases unusual high-frequency fluctuations in accretion rates not seen in other stars. High-frequency fluctuations in XX Cha are notable as they could result from recent disk formation and may indicate a broader stellar regime that could influence our understanding of the development of mass function in young star systems. Moreover, combining these results with earlier findings, a six-year period of accretion rate variability for four stars was determined, revealing distinct patterns of accretion rate behavior and potentially critical information for modeling the development of mass function in young star systems. Lastly, accurate measurements of accretion rates can be made using the new ACCURACY method, which is now publicly available.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning data often includes suboptimal behavior from some agents. Current methods typically attempt to exclude or downweight the data from non-expert agents based on the assumption that most observed trajectories are optimal. This research challenges that assumption by exploring offline learning from positive data, where the majority of observed trajectories are not optimal. A novel model called the Trajectory Shift Adjusted Auxiliary Ratio (TSAR) estimator is presented to handle this issue by focusing learning on the best performing trajectories within each data batch. The TSAR estimator enables efficient offline learning from positive data by leveraging the auxiliary ratio ratio estimation method. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the benefits of the TSAR estimator, showing that focusing learning on the best performing trajectories within each data batch leads to superior performance. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ShangyiNiu/TSAR.

The notion that two or more particles must be simultaneously measured to demonstrate entanglement's genuine nonlocal characteristics has been a widely accepted principle. Contrary to this notion, our research proves that a single particle from an entangled pair can exhibit nonlocal effects on its own, without any need for joint measurement with the other particle. This is achieved by utilizing the particle's own spin entanglement to give rise to a nonlocal guidance effect. This proof serves as an answer to a longstanding question posed by Wiseman in 1998, regarding the possibility of demonstrating nonlocal effects from a single particle of an entangled pair. Our findings also provide a tangible example of single-particle entanglement's significance. If you place the particle at the center of a circle of three parties, one holding the other particle from the entangled pair, then the particle in the center can exhibit both Mach-Zehnder interferometer-based nonlocal effects and the EPR paradox's genuine nonlocal correlation. Our research highlights the immense potential of single-particle entanglement, demonstrating how it can be harnessed to provide guidance to a particle at one end of a communication channel, even when the other particle from the entangled pair is with the sender. This achievement is all the more significant given the practical feasibility of preparing and utilizing such single-particle entanglement, thanks to the availability of robust spin-symmetric protection mechanisms in various physical systems. Our work culminates in a proposed experimental setup, involving a beam splitter followed by a spin-symmetric protection mechanism, which generates single-particle entanglement and results in nonlocal effects in the form of guidance for a particle at one end of a communication channel, even when the other particle from the entangled pair is with the sender. Our findings open the door to exploring single-particle entanglement's immense potential in a variety of scenarios. The integration of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) technology and education holds great promise in creating a safe and efficient transportation system. However, learning models in IoV often lack a centralized authority, making traditional learning methods less effective. Consequently, the potential of integrated systems in facilitating safe and efficient vehicle operations on the road remains unexplored. This survey delves into the underlying technology of IoV education, outlines the challenges it poses, and examines the concept of blockchain-enabled federated education systems. Furthermore, it presents potential applications of these systems in IoV, specifically related to vehicle communication and learning. Finally, this survey also examines the challenges and future directions of such systems in IoV education. This survey is aimed at be contributed to the IEEE access journal. To understand how charge and heat move across a system, especially in the presence of strong fluctuations, is a complex problem that requires accounting for nonequilibrium conditions and geometric features. We investigate the 3D Hofstadter model to examine these phenomena, particularly focusing on how fluctuations and geometry affect each other and impact the distribution of electrons. This leads to surprising results, as the formation of localized distributions of electrons, known as Wannier states, isn't necessarily disrupted by strong nonequilibrium conditions. Instead, the system self-organizes to create tiny regions where equilibrium conditions are established, allowing for a precise analysis of how fluctuations and geometry interact and influence each other. This interplay results in intricate patterns of electron distribution and intricate flows of heat and charge. By exploring this interplay, we identify specific patterns that the system can exhibit, both with and without the presence of boundaries. This includes the formation of closed paths for heat and charge flow, as well as the creation of sharp points and edges within the system. This model demonstrates that complex patterns of charge and heat distribution can emerge from a simple and clean model, and may provide a foundation for understanding similar patterns in more realistic and disordered systems. This includes the effect of defects and irregularities on the distribution of electrons in systems like high-temperature superconductors and certain materials with antiferromagnetic properties. This finding also highlights the unique characteristics of Wannier states and the physical significance of the reciprocal vector that defines the size and behavior of these states. This vector, which is typically considered as a fixed property of these materials, is actually a dynamic property that can vary across different dimensions and fluctuate in response to changes in the system. This is demonstrated by calculating this vector in various configurations and showing how it changes across different dimensions and fluctuates in response to the presence of boundaries and defects. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One notable aspect of text-based games is their slow pace, reaching only a few moves per second, which limits the extent to which virtual agents can be tested for problems requiring a larger number of moves.
Our proposed framework, TextWorldExpress, breaks down the process of creating text-based games and allows for the acceleration of game episodes by generating a compact, symbolic representation of the game environment.
This framework supports the creation of simplified, large-scale text-based games, with the capacity to reach over one million moves per second, which we believe sets a new benchmark for the field.
TextWorldExpress is adaptable to existing text-based game environments and we present two examples of games built using our framework, demonstrating its versatility.
Our analysis of virtual agents' performance in two different textures of the Bumpers game reveals that our framework's symbolic representation is a key factor in achieving high scores. 
Our framework is also suitable for generating hard challenges for virtual agents, as we demonstrate with a difficult version of the Bumpers game requiring multiple attempts to solve. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/sigurtha/textworldexpress.

This research examines the impact of several serial and parallel computation workflow strategies for Bayes factors and identifies a more efficient approach using parallel Markov Chain Monte Carlo. The approach is applicable to a broad range of statistical models and Bayes factor estimation problems. The code for this study is available on GitHub. The research highlights the potential for Bayesian methods to be more computationally feasible in very high-dimensional contexts, where many traditional frequentist methods struggle with performance and accuracy. The findings suggest that Bayesian methods can handle the complexity of real-world data, as seen in a previous application to genomic selection. Discourse markers and indicators are crucial for analyzing and extracting implicit information from conversations, especially in multi-party discussions. However, due to their implicit nature, they are often difficult to detect automatically. Existing approaches rely heavily on manual methods, making the process time-consuming and prone to bias. In this research, we develop a cutting-edge technique for the automated discovery of discourse indicators in conversations, with a focus on discovering signals that reveal relationships between adjacent speech segments. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to a prominent dataset, where it reveals intriguing patterns of discourse indicator usage. Notably, our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, discourse indicators are often used to convey explicit, rather than implicit, information. We also identify instances where their primary function is to present opposing views or to introduce new topics. These outcomes, along with the development of our method, are significant contributions to the field of natural language processing. For researchers interested in exploring this further, we make our approach available as the DiscSense framework. For those interested in examining the intricate web of conversations without the need for explicit graph extraction, we create the DiscSense Explorer tool. This research is an extension of a previous study presented by the team at the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

We investigate a general matrix decomposition problem where the factors must adhere to a specific pattern or sparsity pattern, a problem that has been studied under non-convex and convex settings. This matrix decomposition issue can be seen as an instance of matrix factorization in presence of sparsity constraints, well-studied problems in physics, machine learning, and statistics. A key finding of our work, however, is that once we consider non-convex and non-compact domains, this matrix decomposition problem actually resides in a geodesically convex domain rather than a convex domain. This breakthrough discovery is further illustrated by a global landscape analysis of the matrix decomposition problem along a geodesic, a concept that has not been previously explored in the literature. This analysis reveals that the problem's solution space is divided into three distinct regions: one region where the objective function has an inflection point, another region where the objective function has two local maxima, and a third region where the objective function has no critical points. This groundbreaking result offers our contribution to the field. Moreover, we take advantage of this new insight to modify the well-known reweighted $\ell_1$-minimization algorithm, a state-of-the-art sparse optimization method, to the reweighted $\infty$-minimization algorithm, a state-of-the-art non-convex matrix decomposition method, and provide a theoretical guarantee for the global convergence of this modified algorithm. This guarantee takes the form of a sharp landscape analysis of the matrix decomposition problem. This result is relevant to a broader class of fixed-rank optimization problems, not just matrix decomposition problems. This work was presented at the Thirty Ninth International Conference on Machine Learning held in online format in 2021. Our research aimed to explore the relationship between edge-recognition and the absence of small odd components in a particular class of edge-colored cubic graphs, namely those with a specific tinting of bipartite components. However, we have discovered a counterexample to a previously proposed general property of this type, and it turns out that there are infinitely many examples within this class that are recognizable but cannot exhibit a specific edge-colored 1-factor known as an 'edge-tint'. Moreover, these examples enable us to identify a new concept of strong edge-colorability called strong 2-edge-colorability, and it turns out that this property is equivalent to the absence of a particular component known as a 'double star'. Finally, our findings also imply that another related property known as double-strength is also a more demanding condition than it initially seemed, requiring the absence of a different type of component known as a 'bigon'. Our research thus discovers and explores these two newly identified graph components, the double star and the bigon, and it does so within the specialized context of edge-colored cubic graphs. The property of strong 2-edge-colorability can be realized through a process known as edge-partitioning, and our results conclude with an examination of the relationship between this process and another process known as 2-factorization. The results we have obtained also hold value outside the confines of edge-colored cubic graphs, making them broadly significant. Developing multilingual shared frameworks with integrated semantic structures has gained significant interest recently. However, creating a multilingual shared framework with multiple languages poses a major challenge, specifically developing a common semantic structure across different languages and constructing a framework that incorporates multiple languages. Current methods primarily focus on integrating two languages, with limited exploration of multilingual applications. Our solution introduces a multilingual shared semantic framework with embedded cluster structures, designed to accommodate an arbitrary number of languages. We propose a novel multilingual word representation method, Cluster-Consistent Multilingual Word Representation (CCMWR), which utilizes clustering to capture local semantic patterns and enforce the consistency of these patterns across languages. We also present a strategy for building a multilingual shared semantic framework, demonstrating the flexibility of our approach in handling an arbitrary number of languages. Experimental evaluations on multilingual embedding evaluation tasks and semantic similarity assessment show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods. With the addition of a monolingual baseline for comparison, our method also delivers superior performance in downstream tasks, indicating a strong relationship between in-film similarity and task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/lingua360/CCLMWR.

In the context of federated learning, organizations collaborate to create a centralized model by sharing updates derived from their respective data sets. However, this approach is prone to producing a federated model that simply averages the characteristics of different data sets, thereby compromising security and privacy requirements. Our proposed Federated Discriminative Aggregation (FDA) framework addresses this issue by incorporating a discriminative encoder that separates private data into two distinct components: one that contains private information and another that is comparable to the central dataset. This encoder is optimized during training to prioritize the private component, effectively preventing the leakage of precious private information. Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function called the reverse domain adaptation loss, which enables each participant's model to excel at categorizing the central dataset's data types while minimizing bias towards their own data. By combining these encoder and loss function designs, the FDA framework successfully prevents data sets from being homogenized and mitigates various knowledge integration difficulties. Our experiments on four datasets demonstrate the FDA framework's superiority over the conventional federated learning approach. Moreover, its effectiveness in preventing data set homogenization is evident from the results obtained in another experiment, which involves incorporating new data sets into the model. The FDA framework is particularly useful for integrating knowledge from multiple sources, as it prevents the model from adapting to each new source at the expense of compromising its performance on the other sources. The code for the FDA framework is available at https://github.com/zwang95/FDA.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. However, introducing quantum errors due to nonlinear interactions between elements and substrate coupling hinders large-scale construction. Identifying and managing these errors are dependent on a comprehensive understanding of quantum interactions within Josephson junction-based resonators. This understanding can be acquired through experimental analysis of nonlinear phenomena exhibited by multiple-joint assemblies. In this research, terahertz spectroscopy is used to investigate a planar microwave resonator that contains a pair of Josephson junctions placed in close proximity, 10 microns from a gold metal plate. The distinctive features of this model, including spontaneous emission, Josephson oscillations, and snappy quenching of microwave signals, were studied in different temperature and microwave power conditions. The findings provide valuable information on evanescent near-field interactions between the junctions and the metal surface, and demonstrate the utility of this model in comparing theory and observation, and in validating models of heat transport and nonlinear radiation. The complex nonlinear behavior exhibited here offers promise for investigating cross-talk in quantum circuits and validating models of heat transport and nonlinear radiation. The design of this resonator allows for easy modification of its components, which could facilitate exploration of nonlinear phenomena, such as amplitude-modulated self-oscillations induced by corner modes, and unique nonlinear phenomena exhibited by multiple-joint assemblies. The expertise gained in this research can be applied to other systems that involve cross-talk between elements and a substrate. The terahertz near-field imaging of this system has been well characterized and offers a versatile model for investigating nonlinear phenomena in quantum systems. The resonator's design, which includes a sapphire substrate and a gold plate, allows for easy modification of its components, and the expertise gained in this research can be applied to other systems that involve cross-talk between elements and a substrate. This has led to the discovery of a nonlinear phenomenon called amplitude-modulated self-oscillations induced by corner modes, which occurs when a Josephson junction is placed near the edge of a resonator. This phenomenon was predicted theoretically, but this is the first time it has been observed. The findings from this research are relevant to quantum systems that involve cross-talk between elements and a substrate, and the design of this resonator, which includes a sapphire substrate and a gold plate, offers a versatile model for investigating nonlinear phenomena in quantum systems. Due to the intense heat and corrosive environment on Venus, robotic missions have significant challenges in designing surfaces that can withstand the conditions for an extended period of time. As a result, most Venus surface missions lasts only a few dozen minutes or a few hours on the ground, leaving many uncertainties about the atmosphere's development over a long period of time. To address this knowledge gap, the paper discusses our proposed plans for two types of missions: one that spends several days on the ground and another that orbits Venus for several years. The primary objectives of both missions are to collect data on the atmospheric state over different time scales, with a focus on phenomena seen by previous missions such as the rapid development of the lower atmosphere's temperature and the presence of a swirling pattern of winds at high latitudes. The paper explores various surface and airborne platforms that can be used for these missions, with a focus on designing surfaces and instruments that can withstand the harsh conditions on Venus for an extended period of time. We also examine our results from a preliminary analysis of data collected over a long period of time by the Soviet VEGA 3 lander, with data spanning nearly 107 days. According to the findings, the atmosphere's temperature and composition remain relatively stable with some fluctuations, with the presence of nitrogen heterocycles also confirmed in the atmosphere. These discoveries provide a foundation for our proposed plans for future missions, with a focus on detecting fluctuations in the electron density of the ionosphere and the rotation period of the atmosphere. We also discuss the technical challenges of designing surfaces and instruments that can withstand the conditions on Venus for an extended period of time, with a focus on our proposed procedures and feedback systems for future missions. We believe that our results and discussions on our proposed plans for future missions can be beneficial for scientists and engineers designing surface and airborne platforms for missions to other hostile environments in the solar system. With a focus on the particular challenges of Venus, the paper concludes by highlighting the similarities between this planet and other extreme environments in the solar system, with a focus on Mars, Europa, and Ganymede. The paper also discusses the opportunities for future missions to Venus, with a focus on missions to Ganymede, Europa, and Saturn's moon Titan. The appendix contains additional information about the Soviet VEGA 3 lander's instrument package and the methods used to analyze the data from this mission. The appendix also examines the results from a re-analysis of the data from the Soviet VEGA 1 and VEGA 2 landers, with a focus on the presence of clouds

The non-linear Hawkes model effectively simulates information diffusion dynamics across complex networks by incorporating mutual influence and feedback properties. Despite its predictive capabilities, assessing model accuracy and estimating key parameters proves to be a challenging task. Presently, available methods to evaluate the model's fit to observed data data are largely based on quasi-likelihood maximization, which can result in the fitting process becoming trapped in local optima. Furthermore, these methods lack the ability to assess the model's uncertainty and estimated parameters. This study fills these gaps by introducing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian framework for assessing the model's fit, computing uncertainty for the estimated parameters, and validating the model's validity. This new method is validated through simulations and applied to real-world social media data. The results show that the Bayesian approach outputs better fit estimates compared to the standard method. Moreover, the Bayesian approach reveals intriguing details about the distribution of the network's influence, the non-linearity, and reveals that the network exhibits self-excitation in certain regions. The Bayesian approach's unique insights into the network's dynamics also highlight the coexistence of contrasting diffusion patterns, the impact of the model's non-linearity on the distribution of the network's influence, and the impact of self-excitation on the distribution of the network's influence. The method's limitations are discussed, and possible enhancements to the model, such as adding latent variables, are proposed. The study's findings and the proposed method's results have significant implications for the analysis of complex networks and systems. We investigated the optical and near-infrared light curves and spectral evolution of the rare Type II supernova SN 2020jfo over 360 days to gain insights into its massive precursor star. Comparing its light curves with well-known SNe II, we identified SN 2020jfo as a hybrid with both normal and 1999gi-like characteristics. This distinction is also reflected in its near-infrared light curves, with SN 2020jfo exhibiting a 1999gi-like decline rate in the Ks band within the initial 100 days. Further analysis of SN 2020jfo's light curves using the SN II non-linear radius technique revealed a precursor mass of 19.5 solar masses, with some uncertainty. This is consistent with the results obtained from the semi-analytical model, which indicated a precursor mass of 19.0 solar masses. Additionally, we found SN 2020jfo to have a longer light curve duration than either SN 2013DX or SN 1999gi for the same bolometric energy release. These findings are also reflected in SN 2020jfo's cooling phase temperature evolution, with SN 2020jfo exhibiting the coolest peak temperature among these three SNe II. Combining these indicators, we believe SN 2020jfo exploded with a large amount of hydrogen in its outer layers and had a precursor mass of 19 solar masses. This is unusual for SNe II, which typically explode when their massive precursor stars have masses of 20-25 solar masses. SN 2020jfo's progenitor star is expected to have had a strong stellar interaction, such as mass transfer or binary mergers, which led to its explosive demise. This research highlights the importance of considering the effects of binary interactions in the evolution of precursor stars that give rise to SNe II. Moreover, SN 2020jfo's large light curve extent and slow initial decline rate within the initial 100 days may serve as a marker for similar transients with lower explosion energies. This is also reflected in its near-infrared light curves, with SN 2020jfo exhibiting a 1999gi-like decline rate in the Ks band within the initial 100 days. To greatly decrease the number of photons required to detect a signal in X-ray monitoring tasks, a novel detector concept called the "lobster-eye lens array" has been proposed. This configuration utilizes a grid of pinhole cameras, also known as "lobster-eye lenses," to achieve wide-field coverage. Each lens in the array would be connected to a separate signal channel, significantly increasing the detector's sensitivity in low-flux environments. If each lens has its own amplifier, even in the presence of crosstalk, the system's sensitivity can be optimized for a specific signal source by adjusting the gain on each channel. This concept has been applied to a real detector, the eROSITA X-ray telescope, which will undergo launch in 2023 and will utilize this design to scan the sky for transient X-ray sources. Although primarily developed for this particular telescope, the lobster-eye lens array concept can be adapted for other transient X-ray monitoring applications, such as space-based and ground-based systems, following the eROSITA mission. The prelaunch performance of eROSITA, along with its expected postlaunch performance, will be reviewed. The challenges of background reduction faced by the detector will also be explored. The eROSITA team plans to make raw data publicly available one year after the mission concludes, which will enable researchers to recreate any detected signals and facilitate transient X-ray monitoring across the sky. The scalable design of the lobster-eye lens array detector also makes it suitable for other observational bands, such as optical and gamma-ray monitoring. The system's efficiency in detecting signals can be enhanced further by utilizing machine learning algorithms on the raw data, which would allow it to effectively discover transient sources across the sky for a much longer period than currently possible. The raw data from the eROSITA mission will be accessible through the Strasbourg Sky Catalogue Service. The team behind the eROSITA detector design is open to collaborating with external Transient X-ray Monitoring Projects. The detector's data streaming and storage infrastructure is highly flexible and can be adapted for other large-scale transient monitoring projects in astrophysics. Researchers have long used the cosmic web to understand the large-scale structure of the universe. Specifically, a model based on galaxy distributions, called the cosmic speed field, has been successful in replicating the overall pattern of galaxy movements by incorporating information about the local environment, cosmic expansion, and gravitational attraction. To investigate the relationship between the cosmic speed field and the development of dark matter halos, a deep learning framework was employed to examine the connection between the cosmic speed field and halo masses. The analysis revealed that the speed field's influence on halo formation is primarily evident when considering the mass distribution of halos within a given mass range. Furthermore, the results showed that the speed field's impact on halo formation is more pronounced in the early universe. The findings suggest that the cosmic speed field plays a significant role in shaping the mass distribution of halos, particularly in the mass range $10^{9}-10^{12}M_{\sun}$, and its effect on the universe's matter distribution persists even in the late stages of the universe's evolution. The research highlights the importance of taking into account the complex patterns of the cosmic web and the associated gravity gradients when studying galaxy movements and dark matter halo formation. The results also imply that the cosmic speed field could be a valuable tool for predicting the masses of dark matter halos and predicting the matter distribution in the late stages of the universe's evolution. The study used a simplified model for the cosmic speed field and dark matter halo formation, and future work could build upon these findings using more advanced models. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving convergence in the solution for rotating stars under the theory of general relativity. This method, which uses a quasi-Newtonian framework as a starting point, employs a specific formulation where both the rotation rate and gravitational acceleration are calculated as secondary effects of a primary perturbation. We have successfully applied this method to model both rapidly and slowly rotating stars in both Newtonian and relativistic contexts. Our novel approach offers a distinct understanding of the effects of rotation and gravity and provides a promising foundation for extending our models to more complicated scenarios, such as rotating stars with magnetic fields and exotic matter. Leveraging AI to automatically extract data from diverse documents like invoices, IDs, and receipts holds tremendous potential, especially for businesses and organizations. However, the feasibility of such applications is limited by the high cost of labeling training data. Our innovation addresses this challenge by introducing a method called "Selective Supervision." It employs an unsupervised technique to categorize documents into three groups based on their layout complexity: simple documents that require minimal supervision, complex documents with unusual layouts that need extensive guidance, and intermediate documents that fall in between. The selective supervision approach limits explicit labeling to complex documents and unusual layout areas within the remaining two categories. Our evaluation, spanning nine diverse document types and 12 unusual layout scenarios, shows that even with reduced labeling, our framework achieves high precision for extracting specified data fields. Simply put, our approach allows you to extract data from visually rich documents at a lower cost, making it a significant step towards making such applications more feasible. Our code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/PranavGupta/SelectiveSupervision.

Recent detections of neutron star-neutron star (NSS) and neutron star-black hole (BSH) mergers by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and Virgo Collaborations have opened a new pathway for accessing information and analyzing the universe. However, identifying the merger products, which mostly involve highly spinning neutron stars, proves to be challenging due to the limited training data available for the BSH category. To overcome this difficulty, a new approach is proposed for categorizing neutron star mergers based on their component masses by analyzing the post-merger gravitational wave signals using deep learning networks. This method allows for extracting key characteristics from the signals that are independent of the signal amplitude and phase, thereby enabling reliable BSH/NSS distinctions even for highly spinning neutron stars. Moreover, this research demonstrates that the deep learning networks can be trained to accurately detect characteristic signatures of neutron star mergers, such as neutron star quark stars, which would signal the presence of massive quark matter in the universe. The developed model is then applied to real LIGO-Virgo detections of neutron star mergers, with the results presented in the accompanying paper by the LIGO-Virgo Collaborations. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Apoelzos/NSM-identification. Telecommuting and public health measures implemented globally to combat the COVID-19 pandemic significantly reduced face-to-face interactions in cities. This decrease in urban interactions varied greatly depending on an individual's socioeconomic status, with higher-income individuals interacting more freely than necessary to maintain social distancing, whereas lower-income individuals had more limited opportunities for social engagement due to reduced access to public spaces and increased fear of virus transmission. Consequently, these differences in behavior during the pandemic exacerbated existing disparities in urban interactions, leading to a more pronounced effect on lower-income individuals who already suffered significant social and economic losses as a result of remote work and pandemic-related restrictions. This research uses a computational model to simulate and examine the impact of different levels of telecommuting and virus transmission rates on income inequalities in urban interactions during the pandemic. The results show that a short period of reduced interactions may lead to a temporary decrease in income inequalities, but prolonged periods of telecommuting and high virus transmission rates rates exacerbate existing inequalities in urban interactions, mainly by decreasing the opportunities for social engagement among lower-income individuals who already have limited access to public spaces and urban areas. This research highlights the importance of considering the interplay between public health policies, urban planning, and income inequalities in order to mitigate the negative consequences of prolonged periods of reduced face-to-face interactions in cities. This may be achieved by promoting accessible public spaces that encourage safe social interactions among all socioeconomic groups. The results also emphasize the long-term effects of income inequalities in urban interactions, which persist even after the end of the pandemic, highlighting the necessity for continued support and interventions to address these lingering consequences. The model allows for variations in its parameters and provides valuable policy-related insights, making it a valuable tool for similar research, as well as for local governments and public health officials seeking to understand and manage the impact of the pandemic on their specific community. The model's results can be visualized through animated graphs, which demonstrate the dynamic changes in income inequalities in urban interactions during the pandemic, and can be found at the following link: https://github.com/AmirHajratwala/Urban-Interactions-During-Pandemic. The model has the potential for further development, as well as applications in research and real-world contexts. The code for the model is open-source, transparent, and easily modifiable, allowing for the integration of new features and variables. The formation of massive stars is the most mysterious process in the universe, and the early stages of its development are critical to its overall comprehension.  While it is known that massive stars form from massive molecular cores, the specific path from core formation to star formation remains unclear.  One popular theory suggests that massive stars are born from dense clusters where cores and protostars collide and combine, leading to the formation of massive protostars.  However, there is limited direct observational evidence to support this theory.  Using a groundbreaking method that combines submillimeter interferometry with machine learning, researchers were able to uncover the historical development of a massive protostar called OMC-2 by dissecting a 0.1 parsec region surrounding a young star named $\theta$ Orionis.  They discovered a 0.01 parsec group of small, newly formed protostars that are in the same stage of development as OMC-2, and a massive protostar called ORI-K2 that is more developed.  Further analysis of this data revealed that OMC-2 formed about 30,000 to 40,000 years ago and went through a brief, intense accumulation period before which it had no associated matter.  This is the first direct observation of the initial stages of a massive protostar and reveals that its development was significantly more rapid than expected, taking only about 30,000 years.  Additionally, it showed that dense clusters can form massive protostars through the accumulation of multiple colliding cores, and that these protostars can then collapse into low-mass and high-mass star formation in different proportions, depending on factors such as density and gas removal mechanisms.  This finding provides a clear pathway for massive star formation and offers insights into the short timescales involved, as well as the critical role of dense clusters in forming both low-mass and high-mass stars.  It also raises questions about the likely outcomes of similar collisions in other regions, and suggests that massive protostars may be more common in regions with narrow beam widths than currently observed.  This study used a unique approach to investigate this case, but other methods such as spectroscopic analysis or multi-epoch surveys may provide similar insights in other regions.  Overall, it has significantly advanced our understanding of massive star formation and has identified key areas for future research in this field. Autonomous navigation, especially for underwater robots, is a complex task that requires highly advanced technology. Underwater environments pose significant challenges, including the slow speed of communication and processing, limited power sources, and highly uncertain surroundings. To successfully navigate these conditions, underwater vehicles must utilize conservative movement strategies and prioritize path planning over detailed mapping. Previous research has explored the integration of motion planning and navigation, but it often prioritizes precise mapping over efficient path selection. In this work, we focus on path planning for underwater vehicles equipped with sonar sensors in dynamic, unknown environments. A novel navigation framework called Stratified Navigation Controller has been developed to address this challenge. It leverages level sets to limit the search space for the best navigation path, also integrating slope and curvature information from the sonar data to create a safety buffer. The resulting algorithm is computationally efficient, even for large-scale sonar datasets, and it prioritizes conservative movement in uncertain environments. To validate this research, we conducted extensive simulations and a live demonstration using a ROV with six sonar sensors. The results show that this approach yields robust and safe navigation paths in various underwater scenarios. The code for this research is available online, ready for integration into other underwater navigation projects. The live demonstration data is also publicly accessible. The underlying principle of this research, using level sets for navigation, has been theoretically analyzed to ensure its stability. The analysis reveals that this approach guarantees the existence and uniqueness of the navigation path solution. Furthermore, it has been shown that this method is computationally efficient, with a significant reduction in the search space required for sonar data. Verifying news accuracy has become increasingly difficult in the digital age due to the overwhelming number of articles published online. False news stories, often spread quickly, can result in severe consequences if not addressed promptly. To combat this issue, an effective method for identifying false news articles as they emerge is crucial. This paper presents a novel approach to detecting false news articles based on a text condensation technique that distills high-quality summary sentences from professionally written news articles. We analyze the characteristics of summary sentences and false news articles, revealing that false news articles are more likely to contain sensational language and less likely to include condensed summary sentences. A machine learning model is trained to distinguish between false and genuine news articles using these features. To evaluate our approach, we conduct experiments on two datasets consisting of real and fabricated news articles. The results show that our method outperforms baseline models in both experiments. Furthermore, we investigate the importance of each feature in the datasets and find that the presence of summary sentences and the frequency of sensational language are the most critical indicators of false news articles. To improve the model's performance, we propose a data augmentation technique called text condensation augmentation, which involves training the model on both original and distorted datasets. The experimental findings confirm that this technique enhances the model's performance. The proposed approach and findings can be applied to develop false news detection systems and provide insights for future research into this topic. The code and additional details are available at https://github.com/ghr96 FALSE-NEWS-DETECTION.

This research paper uses mathematical modeling to examine the effects of a curved surface on stochastic temperature fields in a contact scenario. Initially, a warm surface with a specified temperature is positioned on a curved surface, allowing time for the temperature fields within the surface to reach an equilibrium state. We then determine the general formula for the curvature's impact on the temperature fields and related quantities. Specifically, the research yields expressions for the average temperature, heat flux, and second-order moment of the temperature fields across the surface. Furthermore, by modifying the surface's curvature, we are able to observe and analyze the corresponding changes in these quantities. The results demonstrate that the surface's curvature exerts both local and distant effects on the temperature fields. For example, a positively curved surface intensifies the heat flux and raises the average temperature at the surface's center, whereas a negatively curved surface has the opposite effect. The research also reveals that the distribution of the temperature fields across a spherical surface and an infinitely extended plane surface differ substantially. The findings presented can be applied to various situations involving curved surfaces and stochastic fields in contact. The mathematical approach used is applicable to studies of other phenomena, such as the movement of objects on uneven terrain, by modeling the situation as an inhomogeneous random walk. The results demonstrated can be seen as a special case of this approach. The paper concludes by highlighting the importance of considering a curved surface in these analyses. Recent studies using neural networks have successfully entered the age of emotion-based question answering, focusing on natural language inference. However, the potential for these systems to adapt to varying cultural contexts, where question tags may differ, remains unclear. To address this challenge, a framework is established to incorporate a process of semantic tag adjustment, where a neural network is tasked with re-labeling pre-defined tags based on the context of an inquiry. Empirical evidence demonstrates that a simple adjustment model, incorporating a neural semantic decoder, outperforms more complex models. Furthermore, the team discovers that pre-trained language models, when integrated into the decoder, exhibit a significant increase in performance. A notable finding is that the addition of a separate entity recognition module to identify key entities within a sentence does not significantly enhance the effectiveness of the model. A follow-up experiment is conducted to explore the limitations of this framework by expanding the task to incorporate a neural network capable of answering emotion-connected questions, rather than simply adjusting tags. A novel multi-task learning approach is proposed, leveraging a neural network with a switchable output module. The results demonstrate a notable increase in performance when comparing the team's approach to alternative methods used in the community. A straightforward evaluation framework is established to assess the semantic tag adjustment aspect of the model's performance, revealing a connection between the accuracy of tag adjustment and the difficulty of a particular question. A contrasting pattern is observed between intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations, highlighting the influence of question tags on the model's performance. A further analysis into the relationship between the accuracy of tag adjustment and the difficulty of a particular question is conducted, along with an examination of the influence that question tags have on the model's performance in answering emotion-connected questions. A dataset is introduced consisting of text segments that address questions with varying levels of difficulty, along with corresponding tags and emotion connections. The results presented can be replicated by other researchers using the publicly available dataset. The code for the models used in the paper is also provided. The potential applications and extensions of the research are discussed, including the incorporation of multiple emotion connections, the development of a robust dataset, and the exploration of cultural-based question tags. The paper concludes by highlighting the challenges remaining in the field of emotion-connected question answering. For individuals with visual impairments to navigate complex spaces safely and effectively, an innovative map format called HiTMap is being developed to provide an accessible and user-friendly interface for navigation. This new map structure employs advanced topological modeling, incorporating landmarks, paths, and boundaries to accurately represent physical environments. To accommodate various navigation needs, HiTMap enables the inclusion of points of interest, route guidance, and boundary recognition. Furthermore, this format allows for real-time updates and incorporation of sensory data from sonar rangefinders and cameras, offering a multi-modal navigation experience. To demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap, a corresponding algorithm called HiTMapBuilder has been developed to automatically construct these hierarchical maps from LiDAR scan data, while a second algorithm called HiTMapSenser has been developed to integrate camera data with the map, enhancing the navigation experience with visual cues. Experimental evaluations of HiTMapBuilder using real-world LiDAR datasets have validated its precision and efficiency, and the integration of HiTMap with a speech-based navigation system has been demonstrated to provide a safe and effective multi-modal navigation experience for visually impaired individuals. This research presents HiTMap, HiTMapBuilder, and HiTMapSenser as a pioneering effort in developing a groundbreaking map format and supporting frameworks for providing accessible navigation in complex, visually rich environments. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring minute variations in local magnetic fields, specifically the field alterations caused by a nearby, moving absorber in a Michelson atomic interferometer setup. While atomic interferometry effectively detects shifts in gravitational acceleration or gravitational fields, its capacity to measure magnetic field changes, even with high sensitivity, proves more difficult. Overcoming this difficulty requires exploiting the strong magnetic field generated near a absorbing material's edge when it exhibits the Meissner effect in a superconductor. A proposed setup utilizing a superconducting plate within an atomic interferometer detects even minor movements of the plate, thereby sensing the change in local magnetic field induced by the plate's presence. This setup's ability to detect a $1$ Hz shift in the Earth's magnetic field at $5.85$ $\mu$T is demonstrated, highlighting the capacity of atomic interferometry to measure complex local magnetic fields with high precision. Furthermore, this achievement paves the way for utilizing the Meissner effect in superconducting materials to enhance the sensitivity of atomic interferometry to mass variations, providing a means to detect even minimal changes in both local magnetic fields and mass distributions. While initially applicable to searches for dark matter, this technique's utility extends to monitoring local magnetic fields around complex structures, modifying atomic physics experiments that employ magnetic fields, and influencing future applications in matter distribution and spatial variation detection. The engineering requirements and feasible scaling of this setup for larger, real-world implementations are discussed in the paper's companion appendix. The proposed setup has been successfully operational at the Institute of Semiconductors and Microelectronics, Poland, and has led to the publication of one paper by the group. In this work, a parametric model from mixtures is show to be equivalent to a non-parametric model consisting of a probability distribution over parameter spaces. This distribution can be found using Bayesian inference. The result demonstrates that any smooth function of the distribution over the parameter spaces can be estimated using Monte Carlo methods based on random draws from the mixture model parameters. In object-based programming for GPUs, memory allocation must balance concurrency and performance. Current approaches either sacrifice concurrency for faster memory management or trade off memory efficiency for better concurrency, without considering the impact of memory alignment on performance. Additionally, available memory allocators neglect recent GPU features, including the use of virtual memory and the ability to specify preferred memory banks. To address these limitations, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator tailored for object-based programming on GPUs with advanced memory management capabilities. DynaSOAr utilizes a hybrid allocation scheme that leverages both host and device memory, provides efficient memory fragmentation management, offers automatic memory alignment configuration, and takes into account the available memory banks. We evaluate DynaSOAr and other concurrent memory allocators using real-world applications and find that DynaSOAr leaped forward in various benchmarks, outperforming other allocators by a factor of up to 3x. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's performance on a recent NVIDIA Ampere GPU gains a 25% performance improvement compared to the fastest current allocator. To facilitate widespread use, we openly provide DynaSOAr's source code under the permissive Apache License Version 2.0.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This initial principles method, applied to a single magnetic impurity, yields the spectral functions for all relevant states including the Kondo effect, the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) state, and the little--Maxwell--Goppert--Yahr state. When considering two magnetic impurities, the model predicts YSR, two-Goppert--Yahr, and two-Maxwell--Yahr states, depending on the spacing between the impurities and their alignment. This theoretical framework enables the interpretation of experimental data from the YSR states induced by manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface. The results show that a single manganese adatom supports a localized YSR state at the Fermi level, while a pair of adatoms placed far apart will each support a YSR state at the Fermi level, but with their spins coupled in a ferromagnetic arrangement when aligned side by side. In contrast, two adatoms located close to one another will have their YSR states shifted away from the Fermi level and will also exhibit Rabi oscillations between the YSR and Goppert--Yahr states. This theoretical analysis is compared to recent experimental results, where the YSR states induced by manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface were studied using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The experimental data agree with the theoretical predictions, displaying YSR, Goppert--Yahr, and Maxwell--Yahr states for single, side-by-side paired, and closely paired adatoms, respectively. We propose an alternative approach to become the first to measure the elastic production of top-quark pairs. By examining proton-proton collisions at high-energy values, we investigate the potential for detecting forward-scattered protons with large missing transverse momentum. Such an analysis of forward-proton detectors' data would allow for the identification of an isolated lepton signal, indicative of the desired process. Moreover, this approach offers a means to validate inelastic top-quark pair production cross-section calculations via a direct comparison of measured and calculated values. By applying this metric to simulate a massless Dirac cone using qutrits, we find that it is challenging to achieve satisfactory results, however, we do observe the emergence of "sound" in simulations using four-level systems. An alternative strategy called the "truncation expansion" is explored to investigate the behavior of the massless Dirac cone in the low-energy regime. This article explores exponential and analytic functions with integer parameters, demonstrating how these results can be applied to prove the nonexistence of specific function families. These results build upon a 1918 theorem by Hadamard and a 1968 statement by Beurling, which addressed the absence of entire functions with integer zeros. The flow of liquids is opposed by surface tension creating an obstacle, and this challenge is intensified by irregularities on the surface it needs to pass through. While the impact of surface irregularities on flow resistance has been studied extensively, especially in regards to the effect of interfaces, there is a knowledge gap in this area, particularly with respect to the interfaces within dry foams that are highly curved and unstable. Our experiments involving the injection of liquid into dry foams show that surface curvature and instability all contribute significantly to flow resistance, and we have developed a precise metric for measuring this effect. By correlating this metric with the distribution of curvature in the foam, we have demonstrated that the average curvature must be high enough to ensure that the path of least resistance does not bypass the surface, and we have accounted for the additional contribution of surface instability. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between surface tension, geometry, and flow, and they also offer a practical insight for optimizing the pathways of injecting liquids into porous media. Furthermore, our analysis has revealed that the relationship between the work required for injecting a liquid into a foam is much stronger when based on the average curvature rather than the sum of the surface energies along the pathway, and this knowledge can be utilized more efficiently. Lastly, our discovery suggests that the flow through a single interface is more resistant when compared to the flow through a narrow neck in three-dimensional spaces. This research on the flow within dry foams with complex geometry can also be applied to similar problems in biology, such as the flow within the alveoli of the lungs. Lastly, our findings highlight the distinct behavior of dry foams when compared to two-dimensional surfaces and layered materials, and they demonstrate that the flow within these materials cannot be simplified to mere projections of their surfaces.

Early detection of skin carcinoma is critical.  Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks, have made significant progress in image classification tasks. However, these methods often struggle with small dataset sizes, which are common in medical imaging. Additionally, such networks are prone to misclassifying normal skin samples as carcinoma, leading to overdiagnosis. In this study, we used a convolutional neural network to analyze dermoscopy images and assigned an uncertainty score to each sample, which was then used to identify likely carcinoma cases. We evaluated this method on three separate datasets and found that it effectively detects carcinoma in 10% of normal skin samples that were previously undetected. When we combined this method with multi-criteria decision analysis to account for the uncertainty of each sample, it enabled the distinction of 9 distinct skin carcinoma types. This research demonstrates the potential of deep learning to not only detect skin carcinoma but also to differentiate between various carcinoma types and identify normal skin samples that may harbor the disease. This has significant implications for dermatologists and healthcare professionals, who can now leverage this technique for reference purposes to enhance the accuracy of diagnoses. We propose a novel method, calling it Look-ahead Focus for Creation, where the focus is set k steps ahead of the current target position.  We show that setting the focus ahead of the current position can guide the decoder to preferred targets, reducing the distance by approximately 2 steps.  To validate our approach, we conduct several experiments on the NMT architecture with focus, demonstrating that Look-ahead Focus for Creation is effective in reaching high-quality targets, especially in the middle region of the sequence.  We also explore the relationship between our approach and existing techniques, finding that our method complements them by introducing diverse attention weights.  Finally, an analysis of the attention weights with Look-ahead Focus for Creation provides insights into the decoding process, revealing that the decoder's behavior becomes more complex towards the end of the sequence.  We make our code available at https://github.com/ghrua/NMI-Focus-Ahead.

The Framework project, a Java-based application development framework, successfully translated object-oriented programming concepts into grid computing principles. By reinterpreting general programming principles, the Framework team gained a deeper understanding of grid computing, specifically in regard to resource allocation and job management. They achieved this understanding without being bound by the constraints of existing grid middleware. The project's experience served as a foundation for developing the GridBus toolkit, a Java-based grid computing infrastructure. The toolkit features an innovative resource allocation system and provides a simple, high-level programming model for unison execution of tasks across a grid. The GridBus development was influenced by the Framework project's distinctive approach to translating abstract concepts into practical grid applications. The resulting toolkit has been put to use in various real-world applications, including bioinformatics tasks and data intensive simulations. The integration of the GridBus toolkit with other major Java grids has been demonstrated, paving the way for its broader adoption and utilization. The paper discusses the Framework project's novel approach to translating abstract concepts into practical grid applications and the benefits of using the GridBus toolkit in various data and compute-intensive scenarios. The authors' experience suggests that a pure Java grid implementation can be achieved through a translational method that prioritizes the development of abstract concepts over the constraints of existing middleware. The resulting abstract concepts can be validated through real-world implementations of the GridBus toolkit in various domains. The paper's findings are relevant to a broader community working on translational methods and pure Java grids. A combined dark sector model, where both matter and energy experience exponential expansion, is analyzed to determine its implications for the cosmic evolution. By treating the combined dark component as a single entity, known dark energy and dark matter models are generalized. Numerical simulations of this combined model in a $N$-body dark matter simulation are presented, and its effects on galaxy formation are studied. The results indicate that the exponential decay of the dark matter density due to a large $\Lambda$ component does not significantly impact the predicted galaxy mass function, form of galaxy distributions, or star formation activity. However, it does influence the predicted central density of galaxies and their mass. The asymptotic behavior of the model suggests that the matter density may approach a minimum value, which has important implications for the cosmological principles of homogeneity and isotropy at large scales. The model also predicts that there may be galaxies with unusually low central densities on the high-mass end of the galaxy mass function, and these may exhibit distinct properties. The combined dark sector model can be tested through observations of high-mass galaxies on the outskirts of galaxy clusters. The model's parameters can be constrained using galaxy mass functions and cosmological large-scale structure and the properties of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The possibility of the model causing the disappearance of matter on a large cosmic scale in the far future is discussed, and this is compared to the predictions of a $\Lambda$CDM model. The potential for the model to explain phenomena observed at very large cosmic distances is also explored. The code used in the simulations, CDOGT, is described, and it can be used to evolve the combined dark sector in $N$-body simulations. The results and the methodology are further validated by comparing them with existing research, and the potential of the model and its predictions are discussed. The possibility of testing the model through future galaxy surveys and $N$-body simulations in the near future is also explored. We calculate the visible decay branching ratio of J/ψ decays into a photon and an electron/positron pair and find that it exceeds the expected value for one standard model lepton family. This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis method across different dimensional domains. Unlike its scalar counterpart, the method evaluates the singular spectrum of multivariate functional time series. These time series are characterized by observations across various dimensional domains being collected over time. The approach involves applying multivariate state-space models to extract latent processes, whose autocorrelation properties are then determined to identify the underlying structure of the time series. The method has been successfully applied to real-world data sets, including meteorological temperature profiles and electroencephalogram recordings. The results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in determining the underlying dimensions and identifying signals within noisy data. Moreover, the approach has been shown to be robust when there are errors in the dimensionality of the time series. The R package, funFSS, is available to perform the method. The research also highlights potential uses of the method in fields like neuroscience. The approach can be used to analyze multivariate time series with any number of temporal dimensions, any number of spatial dimensions, and with or without missing values in the spatial domains. The method can further handle time series with time-varying dimensional domains. The research presents theoretical foundations for the method in the form of state-space model specifications, model identification using multivariate spectral analysis, the relationship between the model's parameters and the singular spectrum, and the robustness of the method to errors in the time series' dimensional analysis. The appendix contains additional information on the model's parameters, discussion on the model's spatial and temporal dimensions, the robustness of the method to errors in the dimensional analysis, the relationship between the singular spectrum and the model's parameters, the state-space model's specification, the discussion on the method's applicability to time series with time-varying dimensional domains, and a session for reproducing the results presented in the chapter. The research is further illustrated through an example of the method's application to EEG data, the R code for this analysis, and the output of this code. The output of this code is also discussed. The chapter also compares the method with existing approaches to analyze time series with varying dimensional domains. The results of this comparison are presented in the form of a table. The research concludes by outlining potential extensions to the method, the challenges associated with these extensions, the difficulties of implementing the method in fields like finance, and the difficulties of analyzing large datasets with the funFSS package. The chapter also discusses the issues associated with these difficulties and presents a perspective on these challenges. The research further presents a summary of the chapter's main points

This research paper focuses on an one-dimensional random walk model where the walk is subject to external factors that can slow it down or speed it up. The walk's progress is represented by a stochastic process, and we're interested in understanding the long-term behavior of the walk's duration in a given area. Previous studies on similar models found that the walk's duration eventually became stable and consistent across different starting points. In contrast, our results show that the walk's duration can remain unpredictable and vary significantly, even over very large distances, as long as certain conditions are met. These conditions include the absence of extreme slowing factors and a specific distribution of slowing factors that cause the walk to slow down or speed up. Additionally, we found that the walk's duration is influenced by the initial conditions and its own past behavior. Our findings also provide insight into the critical threshold where the walk's duration suddenly becomes unstable and starts varying significantly. Finally, our results can be applied to models that incorporate boundaries or walls by identifying the critical distance where the walk becomes trapped between two points. Our research paper introduces new mathematical techniques and proves several key results about the walk's duration, including its non-persistence and the emergence of sharp boundaries in the walk's behavior. These results demonstrate the complex and dynamic nature of the walk's duration, even in its most basic form. A detailed breakdown of the ICRF plasma generator IShTAR's plasma is provided, focusing on its composition and characteristics. The device's capability to produce long-lasting plasma with a significant amount of neutral atoms has its advantages examined. Furthermore, the paper delves into the investigation of a helicon mode of plasma, facilitated by a helical magnetic field structure. This mode's analysis reveals that it corresponds to a helicon discharge characteristic, marked by a significant amount of electron temperature in comparison to ion temperature. This temperature difference is crucial for reducing electron acceleration during ICRF waves. A proposed modification to the generator aimed at enhancing neutral beam production is also presented. This proposal includes the introduction of a helicon mode in the inner chamber to increase the amount of neutral atoms available for experimentation. Moreover, the paper concludes by highlighting the versatility of the IShTAR device, citing examples such as the possibility of investigating helicon modes in the outer chamber and the availability of neutral beams in the inner chamber. This versatility makes the device an attractive option for multiple applications.

While artificial intelligence has advanced significantly, there's still a challenge incorporating it into pathology imaging, particularly with regards to biopsy slide analysis. A key step in this process is identifying and extracting nuclei from tissue backgrounds, a task that's crucial for further diagnostics, patient classification, and genetic analysis. To enhance the accuracy of this task, a new method called W-Net has been proposed, which leverages two separate convolutional networks to capture both small and large-scale nucleus patterns. Each network operates on a 2D image and produces a binary mask outlining nucleus regions. When applied to datasets containing liver and colon cancer samples, W-Net demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. A particular advantage of this network lies in its simplicity, with limited parameters that facilitate seamless integration into machine-learning pipelines. Moreover, W-Net exhibits robust performance when trained with relatively small datasets, a common issue in pathology imaging. A straightforward way to modify the network has also been presented, allowing it to automate nucleus segmentation based solely on output masks. When evaluated on a dataset with ground-tr truth labels, this modified network showcases an impressive 84% accuracy in correctly classifying nuclei as part of backgrounds or otherwise. A accompanying GitHub repository contains the code and implementation details for this project. The datasets used in this research are publicly available on The Cancer Imaging Archive. The proposed W-Net framework has the potential to contribute to various applications, including cancer diagnosis, tissue classification, and gene analysis, following successful validation of its performance. The results presented have been verified through additional experiments using separate colon cancer datasets, showing the method's broad adaptability. Researchers have successfully applied GCNs across various real-world tasks, yet the lack of insight into their workings hinders further customization and improvement. This study delves into the intricate details of GCNs, proposing an analytical method - matched filtering - that disentangles the convolution operation and reveals the implicit learning mechanisms of GCNs. The study demonstrates its proposal's effectiveness through a series of experiments, showing that the matched filtering method successfully uncovers the underlying structure and characteristics of GCNs. The method also enables the customization of GCNs through parameter tuning, leading to improved performance. The study's findings are further validated across multiple real-world datasets, yielding consistent results. The proposed matched filtering method provides a tangible means of gaining a deeper understanding of GCNs, their structure, and their characteristics, paving the way for further customization and improvement. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying abnormal tissue stiffness. The precision of elastography is significantly enhanced when the system features wide aperture capabilities, yet these setups are prone to systematic errors associated with transducer positioning and motion. A novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method has been developed to tackle this challenge and improve the accuracy of elastography. This approach leverages the advantages of wide aperture systems while minimizing the impact of transducer misalignment and motion artifacts. The VOSA method involves a two-step process: (1) the collection of data from a wide aperture transducer array, followed by (2) synthetic aperture processing using a deliberately introduced displacement between image formations. This displacement enables the derivation of an accurate stiffness estimate via the application of the least squares complex differentiation method. The effectiveness of VOSA has been demonstrated through numerical simulations and clinical trials, showcasing its potential to accurately determine the stiffness of tissues with complex structures, such as prostate glands, by minimising the effects of transducer misalignment and motion artifacts. The development of the VOSA method provides a framework for designing more precise elastography systems, particularly those featuring wide aperture systems with real-time dynamic imaging capabilities. The integration of VOSA-enabled systems with contrast agents and specialized algorithms for complex shear wave data analysis also offers promising avenues for future research. The benefits of VOSA are particularly conspicuous in elastography systems with wide aperture capabilities, real-time dynamic imaging, and contrast agents, and the technique has the potential to contribute to the advancement of various medical applications including, but not limited to, prostate, breast, and liver elastography. The feasibility of VOSA in these areas awaits further investigation by biomedical engineers and medical professionals. Immunizing algorithms from the impact of human error has long been a problem in computer science.  To address this challenge, we propose a new concept - "Rational Pseudocodes."  These pseudocodes represent an advanced form of algorithmic expressions that account for possible human interpretations of the original code.  We can then generate new pseudocodes from a given one by considering all possible human interpretations, effectively making the algorithm more robust.  Interestingly, a short demonstration can be used to generate an entire class of pseudocodes, taking into account the diverse ways humans may interpret it.  This raises the question of whether there are fundamental limits to the size of such pseudocode families.  To investigate this further, we examine a particular case - the pseudocode for binary search - and determine its rational code's basic characteristics, including its complexity.  Furthermore, we establish a significant result - that the proposed framework enables us to determine the intrinsic boundaries of an algorithm, thereby distinguishing it from related but distinct algorithms.  To illustrate this, we generate the rational code for sorting, which reveals a fundamental distinction between merge sort and binary tree sort.  This research was presented at the 58th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science.  There, we explored a specific application - the incorporation of natural language processing - and discovered that it yields a specific form of the W-K Omega matrix, which in turn enables us to determine the intrinsic characteristics of an algorithm, differentiate between distinct algorithms, and even identify the optimal version of an algorithm.  This finding is particularly notable because it allows us to draw a distinction between randomized algorithms and true deterministic algorithms.  In the course of this investigation, we developed a novel theoretical framework - the omega theorem - which may have far-reaching implications for the foundational understanding of algorithms.  There, we examine the underlying structure of algorithms and discover that they conform to a specific pattern, which we refer to as the omega pattern.  This pattern has a tangible representation and can be visualized.  There, we present a specific and general example of this pattern, along with its corresponding graphical representation, the W-K Omega matrix.  This matrix has a distinct and predictable configuration and can be determined using a variety of methods, including natural language processing.  This research demonstrates that the omega pattern and matrix have profound implications for the foundational understanding of algorithms and suggests that algorithms may be more complex than they initially appear.
